values: Record project, deployed release/image, environment, audit period/timezone, accountable owner, decision needed, and evidence root; distinguish intended configuration from deployed state.
Inventory public and private entry points, clients, services, workers, queues, databases, caches, object stores, schedulers, integrations, and manual fulfillment steps.
Map critical user journeys to supporting components, dependencies, data authorities, and failure consequences; distinguish process health from useful service delivery.
Record supported regions, tenants, plans, clients, peak periods, data scale, availability promises, and operating hours; do not assume round-the-clock staffing or multi-region architecture.
Name primary and backup owners for each critical service, dependency, resource, alert, runbook, provider account, and operational decision.
Map shared-host, shared-database, shared-account, shared-region, shared-network, and shared-identity dependencies; identify failures that can affect several applications together.
Inventory monitoring collectors, pipelines, storage, dashboards, paging, status communication, identity, and their own dependencies; identify common failure domains with the application.
Reconcile repository declarations with hosting control planes, system schedulers, containers, external automations, queue repeaters, provider consoles, and billing evidence where access permits.
Record undeclared, ownerless, abandoned, duplicate, and retired resources or jobs; link recurring-work and spend reconciliation to shared module 08.
Record which services inherit verified shared infrastructure controls and which still need application-specific monitoring, permissions, and recovery evidence.
Select applicable checks and specialist handoffs; exclude unsupported platforms/capabilities with reasons and name the evidence gaps caused by unavailable access.
Record each scenario's build/configuration, environment, timestamp/timezone, actor, input, expected result, observed result, method/tool/settings, and sanitized evidence.
Separate source/configuration review, staging execution, production observation, and provider reports; do not claim one proves another environment's behavior.
Trace a representative successful action and a controlled failure from user outcome through telemetry, alert receipt, operator diagnosis, and recovery where applicable.
Record verified sample separately from estimated affected population; explain sampling across services, tenants, regions, deployments, and failure modes.
Distinguish confirmed defects, verification gaps, accepted risks, and opportunities; a missing enterprise-scale tool is not automatically a defect if a simpler workflow meets the requirement.
Deduplicate root causes across operational and specialist audit modules; retain related check IDs and identify one primary owner.
Assess severity, current exposure, confidence, delivery priority, and launch-blocker status separately using realistic impact and documented workarounds.
Keep redacted evidence and operational documents accessible outside the service's failure domain, with approved access, retention, and recovery arrangements.
Reconcile selected check statuses and report coverage, exclusions, unresolved gaps, owners, and acceptance/recheck conditions.
Bound any authorized live verification by target, request rate, duration, cost, impact, cleanup, and stop conditions; use synthetic data and disposable environments for destructive rehearsals.
Select scenarios across outage, partial degradation, silent omission, delayed work, wrong results, monitoring loss, and recovery; do not limit testing to thrown exceptions.
Cover relevant intersections such as provider outage during deployment, monitoring outage during an incident, expired operator access during recovery, and backlog replay after restoration.
Add incidents, near misses, support recurrence, migrations, and known architecture risks to project-specific coverage; expand sampling after inconsistent results.
Define the critical outcomes users rely on, affected audiences, natural usage cycles, and consequences of late, missing, or incorrect results.
Specify each service indicator's numerator, denominator, unit, eligible population, source, aggregation, timezone, and observation window.
Distinguish request availability, latency, correctness, durability, freshness, and end-to-end completion; a successful HTTP response alone does not establish all of them.
Record objective target, rationale, owner, review interval, and contractual relationship; distinguish internal objectives from external service commitments.
Define which requests or jobs are good, bad, excluded, or unknown; justify treatment of client errors, timeouts, canceled work, dependency failure, and planned maintenance.
Check low-traffic, no-traffic, bursty, seasonal, and batch services use meaningful windows and denominators rather than misleading percentages.
Measure relevant tenant, plan, region, endpoint, and client segments without letting a healthy high-volume segment hide a critical smaller outage.
Choose collection and aggregation that reflect real user experience; record gaps from sampling, client blocking, retries, caches, and internal traffic.
Verify indicator data against known successful, failed, slow, and partially completed synthetic actions with authoritative outcomes.
Define objective policy for missing telemetry and delayed ingestion; unknown periods are not silently counted as healthy.
Where using error budgets, define allowed bad outcomes, window, consumption calculation, owner, and responses to rapid or sustained consumption.
Verify objective breaches influence release, capacity, reliability, or investigation decisions; avoid collecting objectives with no accountable action.
Distinguish liveness, readiness, startup, dependency health, and user-facing synthetic checks; document what each establishes and what it omits.
Verify a process that is running but unable to serve useful work is detected by an appropriate readiness or user-facing check.
Ensure health checks have suitable timeouts, frequency, thresholds, and hysteresis; they do not create restart loops or overload a failing dependency.
Check whether dependency failures should remove an instance, mark partial degradation, or preserve a fallback; avoid one dependency outage unnecessarily removing all capacity.
Run appropriate external monitoring outside the application's failure domain; record network, DNS, TLS, identity, and provider dependencies of the probe.
Verify probes exercise the intended host, route, region, authentication state, and useful response rather than only a cached landing page or redirect.
Test expected content/state, not only status codes; maintenance pages, login redirects, and empty success responses do not pass a useful-service check by accident.
Use synthetic credentials/data with scoped permissions, cleanup, rotation, and cost bounds; probes do not create real purchases or contact unintended recipients.
Cover relevant geographic/client entry points and distinguish regional network failures from global service outage using independent evidence where practical.
Verify health endpoints reveal no unnecessary secrets/topology, stay inexpensive, and have controls suited to their public/private exposure through specialist security review.
Define expected completion/freshness for critical scheduled jobs, reports, syncs, backups, notifications, and materialized data; missing execution triggers detection without an exception.
Check last-started, last-successful, completion deadline, runtime, overlap, and missed schedule separately; starting is not proof of useful completion.
Test disabled scheduler, stalled worker, missed trigger, success with zero useful output, and wrong-environment execution using controlled fixtures.
Account for business calendars, DST, local time, approved pauses, and planned infrequent execution without suppressing genuine stale-work failures.
Verify successful completion reflects validated output or reconciliation, not merely a process exit or heartbeat emitted before work finishes.
Monitor backup age and last verified restore separately; operational freshness does not prove the backup can restore correct data.
Check customer-visible freshness/status labels reflect actual data age and partial outages; degraded service is communicated truthfully.
Review objectives after architecture, audience, workload, dependency, or promise changes; retain the definition/version needed to interpret historical results.
Capture meaningful client, API, server, worker, scheduler, integration, and administrative failures; verify controlled examples reach the actual monitoring backend.
Use structured records with timestamp/timezone, service, environment, release, operation, stage, outcome, severity, duration, and appropriate correlation identifiers.
Trace a user action across ingress, application, queued work, provider calls, persistence, and callback where relevant; asynchronous boundaries retain safe correlation.
Distinguish original operation, retry, batch, item, request, job, and external event identities so duplicate effects and replay can be diagnosed.
Record successful critical transitions as well as failures when needed for reconciliation; do not infer success merely from the absence of exceptions.
Check caught exceptions, rejected promises/tasks, background crashes, startup failures, and shutdown failures are visible with useful context.
Preserve actionable error classification and causal chain without repeatedly logging the same stack at every boundary; grouping distinguishes materially different failures.
Verify source maps/debug symbols and release mapping where used, with access controls; production errors resolve to the actual deployed version.
Check timestamps, clock synchronization, duration measurement, ingestion time, and out-of-order events; diagnose clock skew rather than presenting a false sequence.
Verify instrumentation does not silently omit failed paths, pre-auth failures, cold starts, streaming errors, or work completed after the client disconnects.
Where tracing is needed, inspect meaningful spans for request, dependency, database, queue wait, and processing; separate waiting from execution time.
Propagate trace context across supported boundaries with documented trust rules; untrusted incoming correlation data does not enable spoofed authority or uncontrolled storage.
Document sampling strategy, loss, and limitations; rare/slow/failed requests needed for diagnosis remain discoverable by tracing or another adequate evidence source.
Check traces, metrics, and logs link to the same service/environment/release and time interval; unrelated events are not joined merely because identifiers collide.
Verify trace/error instrumentation captures final outcome for partial responses, canceled streams, retries, and provider timeout after a possible remote success.
Check profiling or deep diagnostics, if used, have bounded duration, overhead, access, and retention; avoid enabling costly capture indefinitely.
Give users/support a safe diagnostic reference that can locate the relevant event without revealing credentials or internal details.
Inspect actual payloads for secrets, tokens, cookies, credentials, payment details, sensitive prompts, and unnecessary personal data; verify redaction before export where required.
Check URLs/query strings, headers, stack locals, attachments, screenshots, session replay, and provider error bodies as potential sensitive-data paths.
Restrict access by role/environment/tenant as needed; privileged telemetry queries, exports, and configuration changes have appropriate accountability.
Define retention, deletion, archival, legal hold where applicable, and provider destinations by signal/data class; verify actual policies rather than relying only on documentation.
Verify telemetry transport/storage credentials, rotation, encryption requirements, regional handling, and third-party processing through the security/privacy and legal modules.
Bound untrusted values, escape log content appropriately, and prevent multiline/control-character input from obscuring event attribution or operational interpretation.
Check temporary debug logging has an owner, expiry, approved data scope, and rollback; it does not persist unnoticed after an incident.
Inventory agents/collectors/exporters, buffers, transforms, sampling, indexes, storage tiers, dashboards, and alert queries; name ownership at each stage.
Monitor telemetry ingestion delay, dropped/rejected records, queue/buffer saturation, exporter errors, and backend query availability independently of application errors.
Test telemetry backend outage or blocked egress in a safe environment; application behavior, bounded buffers, disk use, and backpressure follow the intended policy.
Verify restart/reconnect behavior, duplicate delivery, buffer loss, and late events; disclose gaps rather than reconstructing invented continuity.
Bound log volume, record size, trace volume, metric dimensions, retention, indexing, and export costs; identify noisy loops and unexpected cardinality growth.
Check rotation and quotas prevent log files or telemetry buffers exhausting application disk/inodes; diagnostic evidence remains obtainable under pressure.
Verify collectors do not unintentionally duplicate ingestion across replicas, agents, environments, or overlapping integrations.
Confirm telemetry failure is detectable through an independent route proportionate to risk; a silent broken monitor does not report itself healthy.
Test a known diagnostic question against retained data and actual query permissions; chosen retention/sampling permits the required investigation window.
Record instrumentation overhead and cost at representative workload where material; operational visibility does not consume uncontrolled service capacity.
Define traffic, error, latency, completion, freshness, and saturation metrics relevant to each critical service; record unit, source, owner, labels, aggregation, and window.
Distinguish event time from scrape/ingestion time, absent data from zero, and failed collection from healthy inactivity.
Verify counters, rates, gauges, histograms, resets, units, and aggregation against known synthetic activity; restarts do not create misleading negative or inflated rates.
Show appropriate latency distribution and slow-tail behavior, sample count, and workload context; do not hide tail failures behind a global average.
Check histogram boundaries/resolution suit operational thresholds and actual workload; record approximation and aggregation limits.
Verify dashboards filter the correct environment, region, service, deployment, tenant class, and period; staging noise does not contaminate production conclusions.
Link dashboards to objective definitions, alert rules, relevant logs/traces, runbooks, and owner; annotations identify deployments, incidents, maintenance, and data gaps.
Test no-data, partial-data, delayed-data, timezone, daylight-saving, and access-denied states; displays do not imply valid health from an empty panel.
Check aggregation does not hide minority tenant/region failures, error bursts, or capacity imbalance; drill-down is available without exposing unnecessary customer data.
Verify dashboard/query versions, permissions, backups or reproducible definitions, and a usable fallback during the primary dashboard's outage.
For self-hosted services, monitor CPU saturation/throttling, memory pressure, process/container restarts, and out-of-memory termination; identify the affected workload.
Monitor disk space, inodes, I/O latency, filesystem errors, mount availability, and relevant storage quotas; capacity alerts leave realistic remediation time.
Check network reachability, connection errors, bandwidth, egress, DNS/TLS failures, and load-balancer behavior where operated by the team.
Measure database connection pool use/wait, slow queries, lock contention, replication lag, storage growth, and resource ceilings relevant to the deployed engine.
Monitor queue depth and oldest age, arrival/completion rates, in-flight work, retries, dead letters, and consumer availability; depth alone does not establish latency or health.
Check cache availability, hit/miss behavior, evictions, memory, stale data, and dependency load on cache loss; a high hit rate does not prove correct data.
Track object count/bytes, versions, temporary uploads/exports, lifecycle cleanup, retrieval/egress, and provider quotas where material.
Identify shared-host noisy neighbors and per-application resource attribution; a healthy host average does not hide one saturated workload.
Monitor platform-specific ceilings such as file descriptors, process/thread count, port exhaustion, connection caps, and build/runtime limits where they can constrain service.
Track capacity lost to backups, maintenance, deployments, scans, compaction, or batch jobs; routine work does not unexpectedly starve critical traffic.
Record current typical/peak workload, forecast basis, headroom, bottleneck, and capacity owner; estimates identify uncertainty and expected growth rather than inventing demand.
Verify autoscaling bounds, triggers, warm-up, scale-down, minimum capacity, and dependency constraints where used; scaling does not simply move the bottleneck or cost spike.
Test approved overload/degraded-mode behavior with bounded workloads; admission control, queues, timeouts, and recovery protect useful service.
Check capacity and cost after failover or loss of one component where redundancy is promised; document reduced capacity and the scope actually rehearsed.
Reconcile resource usage and billed units with provider reports and cost-module inventories; missing billing access remains a gap, not proof of zero spend.
Track relevant total spend, spend velocity, unit cost per useful outcome, unusual egress, repeated failed work, and unallocated shared cost.
Monitor telemetry/cardinality, CI/build, previews, external automation, retained backups, abandoned resources, and idle-but-billable services as applicable.
Define budget/capacity alert delay, recipient, decision, and containment route; distinguish advisory warnings from hard enforcement through shared module 08.
Verify alerts anticipate contractual limits, certificate/domain renewal, license expiry, prepaid depletion, and storage exhaustion when these can interrupt service.
Review forecasts and dashboards after launches, migrations, pricing changes, incidents, and major data growth; remove obsolete panels without losing necessary coverage.
Inventory alert rules with service, failure mode, source/query, threshold/window, severity, recipient, owner, runbook, and required action.
Map critical outcomes, silent missing work, resource exhaustion, dependency failures, spend, and relevant security changes to an appropriate detection/response route.
Separate urgent pages, working-hours tickets, informational notices, and trend reviews based on action urgency and impact rather than raw log level.
Set thresholds from objectives, workload, failure consequence, and remediation time; avoid importing arbitrary universal values.
Check both rapid severe deterioration and sustained smaller failure where material; objective/budget-based alerts have explicit windows, denominators, and action policy.
Define no-data, missing series, delayed ingestion, scrape failure, and telemetry outage behavior; absence of data does not silently clear a real incident.
Verify low-traffic denominators, expected idle periods, batch schedules, business calendars, and cold start do not generate misleading alerts or conceal failures.
Include environment, service, scope, start time, impact, safe diagnostic links, release context, and next action in the alert without leaking secrets or unnecessary customer data.
Verify alert queries and dashboards agree on scope/window/units; a responder can reproduce the condition from accessible evidence.
Test threshold crossing, sustained failure, recovery, and relapse using bounded synthetic fixtures; retain timestamps through detection and receipt.
Route alerts to a current accountable person or staffed channel; former staff, personal-only accounts, and unmonitored inboxes are not the sole route for essential incidents.
Define coverage hours, primary/backup, acknowledgement target, escalation path, and out-of-hours limitation; promises match actual availability.
Test real receipt through the configured production alerting route using an explicitly labeled harmless test; vendor preview/configuration validation alone is insufficient.
Test absent acknowledgement, unreachable primary, expired contact, invalid token, and notification-provider failure with approved scenarios; fallback reaches someone who can act.
Verify mobile/email/paging settings, quiet modes, device changes, channel membership, and platform permissions do not defeat promised urgent delivery.
Check acknowledgement, assignment, escalation, resolution, and handoff semantics; acknowledging a page does not automatically mean the incident is mitigated.
Record end-to-end detection, routing, receipt, acknowledgement, and action times separately; do not report a single ambiguous response metric.
Keep emergency contacts, provider escalation, and runbooks accessible if the app, main network, identity provider, or primary collaboration tool fails.
Verify an independent route detects failure of the alerting pipeline proportionately to risk, including dead-man checks where appropriate.
Group related symptom alerts while preserving affected services/tenants and useful context; deduplication does not merge unrelated incidents.
Use inhibition/dependency rules carefully so a parent outage reduces noise without suppressing independent security, data-loss, or recovery failures.
Check flapping, short spikes, repeated retries, and alert storms; persistence/hysteresis and rate limits reduce noise without delaying urgent detection beyond the agreed window.
Define maintenance/silence scope, owner, reason, start/end, and automatic expiry; deployment maintenance does not mute unrelated services indefinitely.
Verify alerts recover only after the real condition resolves; missing telemetry, manual closure, and a restarted collector do not fabricate recovery.
Review alert volume, actionable proportion, duplicate pages, missed incidents, time to action, and responder workload using actual patterns.
Remove or retune obsolete rules and identify missing ones after incidents; disabling a noisy alert includes an alternate detection route or documented risk acceptance.
Provide responders the permissions, tools, context, and training needed for the expected action; a page to someone unable to access the system is not effective coverage.
Test rotation/handoff, leave, illness, owner departure, and one-person-team fallback; record realistic external help or accepted coverage gaps.
Check escalation avoids dependence on the same failed account, provider, network, or device wherever practical.
Review coverage and contact accuracy after staffing, vendor, identity, application, and phone/device changes; retain evidence of the latest delivery rehearsal.
Identify deployed source revision, artifact/image digest, runtime, migration state, feature flags, and critical configuration without exposing secrets.
Trace the running artifact to its build and release record; distinguish a rebuild of a source revision from promotion of the exact same artifact.
Document build, verification, approval where required, deploy, smoke check, observation, and recovery steps with accountable operators.
Separate staging/test/live credentials, resource names, provider accounts, endpoints, and data; verify deployed configuration points to the intended environment.
Check failed builds, unavailable registries, partial uploads, missing artifacts, and expired deployment credentials produce visible failure rather than a false successful release.
Verify release metadata links telemetry and customer-visible failures to the actual instance/version during mixed-version deployments.
Ensure necessary deployment definitions and known-good artifacts remain recoverable with appropriate access if the primary workstation or build service is unavailable.
Inventory required environment/configuration values, source, owner, defaults, reload/restart needs, and validation; missing critical values fail safely and visibly.
Record intentional environment differences and detect meaningful drift between versioned declarations and deployed settings.
Verify secret rotation, expiry, revocation, overlapping validity where needed, distribution, restart behavior, and application recovery through specialist security review.
Prevent logs, build output, health pages, diagnostics, and release records exposing secrets; reference secret versions/identities rather than values.
Check configuration changes receive proportionate validation, change attribution, rollback/containment, and telemetry annotations like code changes.
Test feature-flag defaults, eligibility, stale clients, conflicting combinations, control-plane outage, and removal/expiry; disabled UI alone does not stop backend work.
Verify emergency controls and safe fallbacks do not silently enable an unintended provider, debug mode, public access, or unlimited spending.
Test startup/readiness, warm-up, dependency initialization, startup migration, and insufficient-capacity behavior; instances receive traffic only according to the intended health policy.
Verify draining and graceful shutdown for requests, streams, workers, locks, leases, and in-flight jobs; termination behavior is observable and documented.
Test old/new application versions with relevant schema, message, API, and cache formats during rollout and rollback.
Rehearse data migrations with representative scale, runtime, locks, failure midway, restart/resume, and irreversible steps in a disposable environment.
Verify migrations and schedulers execute with the intended coordination across replicas; deployment does not create duplicate jobs or competing destructive changes.
Check canary, rolling, blue/green, or simple replacement behavior only where used; traffic selection, observation, and abort conditions match the chosen strategy.
Test partial rollout, unhealthy new instance, old instance remaining active, and deployment cancellation; the operator can identify and reconcile actual state.
Verify static assets, CDN caches, client bundles, service workers, and API versions remain compatible or present an explicit supported refresh path.
Check simultaneous deployments, operator retries, locked pipelines, and emergency changes; competing actions do not leave an unknown release/configuration state.
Verify scheduled jobs, repeaters, external automations, and old environments are not duplicated by cutover; check actual deployed scheduling sources.
Verify supported low/no-downtime claims under representative traffic, including database and worker transitions; document what was not rehearsed.
Recover a known-good release using the actual operator route in a safe rehearsal; record access, artifact/configuration availability, steps, duration, and smoke results.
Identify rollback limits for schema/data changes, external messages, charges, deleted records, and irreversible side effects; define forward recovery or compensation where needed.
Define automatic/manual rollback triggers and decision authority; telemetry delay or missing metrics does not falsely certify a canary healthy.
Run bounded post-deploy checks for useful user journeys, background work, data state, critical integrations, errors, and alerting; observe long enough for relevant delayed effects.
Assign OS/runtime/dependency/platform patch ownership, supported-version tracking, update validation, failed-update detection, and required restart/reboot handling.
Rehearse certificate, runtime, database, operating-system, and provider upgrades proportionately, including compatibility, backups, rollback limits, and operator availability.
Track emergency/manual changes back into versioned automation or documented configuration; later reconciliation does not silently undo an essential mitigation.
Retire old deployments, previews, temporary flags, credentials, jobs, and billable resources only after dependency checks; verify they stay retired after redeployment/reconciliation.
Close the change record with actual version, times, outcome, incidents, residual risks, and follow-up owners rather than only the pipeline's success state.
Define incident criteria and impact-based severity examples for outages, degradation, data integrity, security/privacy, failed money flows, abuse, and unexpected spend.
Identify declaration, incident lead, technical responders, communications, provider escalation, and decision authority; include backup and small-team coverage.
Maintain accessible runbooks for the critical failure modes in scope, including outage, backlog, disk full, provider failure, credential compromise, restore, payment drift, and spend spike.
Each runbook includes symptoms, impact checks, prerequisites/access, safe diagnostic steps, mitigation, stop conditions, recovery validation, escalation, and owner/review date.
Distinguish read-only diagnosis from actions that delete, replay, charge, restart, fail over, or expose data; include appropriate authorization and bounded execution.
Verify emergency documentation, contacts, credentials/recovery methods, and communication routes remain available during app/host/network/identity outage.
Triage using user impact, blast radius, time of onset, recent changes, evidence confidence, and ongoing harm; avoid assuming the first correlated deployment is the cause.
Separate confirmed facts, hypotheses, unknowns, and actions in a timestamped timeline; preserve relevant redacted evidence before destructive recovery steps.
Establish a working incident channel and decision log with access suited to the sensitivity and outage scenario; do not rely solely on the failing application.
Test scoped/global feature, account, traffic, integration, worker, and cost stop controls where needed; controls cover all relevant entry points and replicas.
Verify kill switches persist or revert according to an explicit policy across restart, rollback, failover, and configuration reconciliation; operators can confirm the actual state.
Check containment preserves recoverable user work and essential security/admin access while limiting harm; user messages reflect the temporary limitation.
Validate restart, scale, drain, rollback, failover, replay, and restore actions against dependencies and data invariants through the relevant specialist audits.
Prevent competing responders from making conflicting changes; record operator, time, reason, target, result, and reversal/compensation route for material actions.
Define when to stop investigation and mitigate ongoing harm, and when evidence preservation or irreversible consequences require specialist involvement.
For security/privacy incidents, use the security response and legal assessment path, including jurisdiction-specific notification review by accountable qualified people.
For financial/usage drift, reconcile authoritative state before replaying payments, refunds, provider work, or entitlement updates; route correctness to modules 08 and 13.
Verify controlled reopening after containment checks budgets, permissions, dependency health, backlog, and retry storms rather than simply re-enabling everything.
Assign communication owner, audience, channel, update cadence, approval needs, and fallback; expectations fit impact and actual staffing.
Keep an appropriate incident/status route reachable outside the application's failure domain; test update access during relevant identity/hosting failures.
Communicate confirmed scope, symptoms, workarounds, current action, and next update time; estimates and unresolved causes are identified as uncertain.
Avoid disclosing credentials, exploit details, unnecessary personal data, or unverified attribution in status pages, support scripts, and internal broad channels.
Align customer support, sales/account teams, provider tickets, and public status so users receive consistent information without claiming recovery before validation.
Distinguish service restored, backlog cleared, data reconciled, financial corrections complete, and incident closed; report residual effects honestly.
Define impact, detection, acknowledgement, mitigation, restoration, reconciliation, and closure times separately with timezone and evidence.
Review contributing conditions, safeguards that worked/failed, alternate explanations, and organizational constraints without reducing the cause to individual blame.
Assess missed/late detection, alert noise, permission gaps, runbook accuracy, communication, and recovery friction alongside the triggering technical defect.
Assign concrete prevention/detection/recovery actions with owner, due date, expected benefit, and observable acceptance; distinguish necessary fixes from speculative expansion.
Verify completed actions using focused evidence and update scenarios/runbooks; a written postmortem alone does not resolve recurring failure.
Track repeat incidents, near misses, customer impact, unresolved action age, and response workload; avoid comparing ambiguous response averages across unlike incident classes.
Rehearse representative incidents, including absent primary responder and unavailable collaboration/monitoring; record which steps were discussed versus actually executed.
Share appropriately redacted lessons, update ownership and training, and confirm accepted residual risks have an accountable expiry/review trigger.
Define important failure scenarios, acceptable recovery time, acceptable data-loss window, scope, owner, and business rationale; distinguish targets from measured rehearsal results.
Map recovery dependencies including identity, DNS, certificates, secret storage, artifacts, databases, object storage, queues, providers, documentation, and billing access.
Record authoritative data sources and recovery order; restored application, cache, index, queue, and external state do not silently disagree.
Identify single failure domains and necessary off-host/off-account/off-region copies proportionate to scoped risk; do not assume multiple regions are mandatory.
Verify backup schedules, completion, age, size plausibility, retention, access, encryption/key availability, and failure alerts from actual operational evidence.
Verify backups exclude unintended secrets or contain them only under approved handling; recovery credentials/keys are not available solely inside the failed system.
Track the last successful restore rehearsal and what data/components it covered separately from the last successful backup run.
Include configuration, infrastructure definitions, certificates, artifacts, object data, and provider/account recovery as applicable; database backup alone may omit the usable service.
Check retention/cleanup failures, full backup destinations, expired access, missing encryption keys, and provider limits are detected before restoration is needed.
Document replacement-environment prerequisites, permissions, capacity, runtime versions, connectivity, and expected cost before a major recovery.
Restore representative backups into an isolated environment and validate records, relationships, files, important user journeys, and data invariants through module 09.
Record restore start/end, operator involvement, dependencies, data-loss estimate, validation evidence, and deviations from the target.
Verify restored services do not unexpectedly email customers, charge providers, replay purchases, run legacy jobs, or expose copied production data.
Test relevant point-in-time recovery, corrupt/missing backup, interrupted restore, and unavailable primary operator using safe fixtures where these risks apply.
Confirm restored identities, secrets, permissions, configuration, and feature flags are valid and do not undo later revocation or containment decisions.
For failover, verify authoritative writer/traffic ownership, fencing or equivalent safeguards, replication lag, application routing, and split-brain prevention through specialist review.
Validate degraded-mode behavior and reduced capacity during failover; users and operators know what remains unavailable or stale.
Rehearse DNS/cache/connection propagation, certificate coverage, external allowlists, callback endpoints, and monitoring changes required by recovery/cutover.
Define failback criteria, data reconciliation, operator authority, and verification; returning to the original environment does not create competing active schedulers or writers.
Verify monitoring, alerting, backups, cost controls, and support access are active in the recovered environment before declaring normal operation.
Diagnose backlog using oldest age, arrival/completion rate, retry state, dead letters, dependency limits, and per-tenant fairness rather than depth alone.
Define pause/drain/resume controls, allowed concurrency, backpressure, processing order, and who may replay or delete work.
Inspect replay candidates for current permissions, entitlement, quota, expiry, deletion, and user cancellation; stale queued work is not automatically still authorized.
Check idempotency, duplicate detection, ordering, and external-outcome reconciliation before replay through reliability/integration/payment modules as applicable.
Test recovery after timeout with unknown remote outcome; operators can reconcile provider state before repeating a charge, send, purchase, or costly generation.
Bound replay by rate, concurrency, cost, scope, and stop conditions; recovery does not overwhelm dependencies, trigger abuse controls, or starve new critical work.
Verify partial replay, poison messages, repeated failure, skipped items, and compensating actions are visible with item-level outcome/accountability.
Reconcile restored database state with newer provider effects, emails, refunds, entitlements, search indexes, analytics, and retained exports where relevant.
Confirm backlog cleared means expected useful work is completed/reconciled or explicitly abandoned, not simply that queue messages were deleted.
Close recovery with validated service/data state, residual customer actions, removed temporary access/resources, updated runbooks, and a follow-up owner.
Inventory domain/DNS, repositories, hosting, deployment, registries, database, monitoring, alerting, email, payments, billing, secrets, and other critical provider accounts.
Verify organization-controlled ownership, renewal/payment routes, recovery contacts, and at least one authorized backup administrator where needed; avoid dependence on one person's private account.
Map normal operator roles to least-privilege tasks and environments; staff can diagnose and mitigate without routine untracked full-access credentials.
Verify strong authentication, scoped credentials, recovery factors, and revocation through security review; record access availability without copying secret values into the audit.
Rehearse emergency/break-glass access with appropriate authorization, logging, scope, expiry, and post-use review; it does not become an unaudited bypass.
Test access when the primary identity provider, operator laptop, password manager, network, or main phone is unavailable where these are material dependencies.
Verify operator onboarding, role changes, departure, contract expiry, and dormant access removal include provider consoles, monitoring, paging, CI, SSH, secrets, and recovery contacts.
Rehearse lost/stolen operator-device response: revoke sessions/keys/device access, assess exposed credentials, preserve appropriate evidence, and restore authorized access independently.
Check administrative actions and access to sensitive telemetry are attributable and reviewable; shared accounts have documented necessity and compensating accountability where unavoidable.
Verify account lockout, billing suspension, provider review, expired card, lost domain, and account compromise have an escalation/recovery path proportionate to risk.
Maintain a concise service ownership map, architecture/dependency map, deployment route, known limits, runbooks, provider contacts, and escalation expectations.
Keep authoritative documentation versioned or otherwise change-tracked, with owner and review trigger; secrets use approved storage references.
Verify documentation remains reachable during the relevant host, application, identity, and collaboration-tool outage with suitable confidentiality controls.
Have an authorized backup operator follow a critical runbook without relying on the primary person's laptop or undocumented memory; record actual friction.
Identify essential manual fulfillment, data correction, renewal, reconciliation, and support steps; define absence cover and failure detection.
Distinguish discussion/tabletop, tool walkthrough, staging execution, and production evidence in training and rehearsal records.
Assign review/patch/renewal ownership for OS/runtime, dependencies, certificates/domains, licenses, provider changes, secrets, and operator devices as applicable.
Maintain versioned/reproducible infrastructure and configuration or an equivalent proportionate record; detect material drift and reconcile intentional manual changes.
Review recurring jobs and external automations for necessity, schedule, owner, timezone, duplicate instances, credentials, monitoring, and cost through module 08.
Retire obsolete jobs/resources with dependency checks, residual queued-work handling, restart/redeploy/reconciliation checks, and billing confirmation before declaring completion.
Verify temporary debug rules, incident access, maintenance silences, migration resources, preview environments, and emergency flags have owners and expiry/cleanup evidence.
Record relevant provider commitments, support tier, service limits, planned changes, renewal dates, and escalation route; no contractual requirement is assumed universally.
Confirm data/log retention, deletion, preservation, audit evidence, and incident notification obligations have accountable project reviewers through modules 01 and 11.
Check provider portability/exit and company handover needs against actual risk, including data export, resource inventory, credentials, recovery, and financial obligations.
Define a risk-appropriate operating cadence covering objective breaches, incidents, noisy/missing alerts, capacity, spend, access, maintenance, and recovery evidence.
Track accepted remediation actions with owner, date, dependency, evidence-based acceptance, and focused recheck; aging tasks and accepted risks receive explicit review.
Review responder workload, staffing coverage, manual toil, and recurring operational mistakes; prioritize changes that reduce real risk or repeated work.
Validate automation before expanding privileges or removing human checks; manual fallback and failure detection remain proportionate to consequence.
Distinguish operational control effectiveness from tool adoption, document count, dashboard count, or completed training; use demonstrated outcomes and limitations.
Trigger focused reassessment after major release, migration, ownership/provider change, incidents, new markets, new data classes, or significant workload growth.

For a single VPS/shared host, test external useful-service detection, per-app resource attribution, host saturation, disk/inode exhaustion, provider-console access, restart ordering, and off-host recovery evidence.

For containers or Coolify-like platforms, verify desired versus actual deployment, image identity, crash/restart loops, health routing, persistent mounts, build failures, orphan containers, and platform-control-plane recovery.

For orchestrated clusters, verify scheduling/capacity failures, rollout health, service routing, node loss, storage attachment, workload identity, control-plane dependence, and version-compatible recovery as scoped.
For managed PaaS/serverless, check invocation failure, cold start, concurrency/timeout ceilings, throttling, region/provider incident, deployment drift, and logs that survive instance disappearance.
For edge/CDN/static hosting, verify DNS/TLS, cache/invalidations, stale assets, origin failure, edge/origin disagreement, geographic degradation, and an external useful-content probe.

For multi-region or redundant systems, verify traffic steering, data authority, replication lag, split-brain safeguards, regional capacity, failover/failback, and monitoring independence only to the promised level.
For scheduled jobs, test missed start, late finish, silent zero-output success, overlap, timezone/DST, disabled scheduler, duplicate replicas, old environment, and restart/redeployment resurrection.
For queues, verify oldest age, dead letters, poison message, lease/visibility expiry, worker crash, retry amplification, fairness, safe replay, and current authorization of stale work.
For batch/ETL/reporting, check input arrival, partition coverage, schema drift, partial completion, reconciliation, lineage, late data, idempotent rerun, and downstream freshness.

For databases, test operational detection/diagnosis of connection exhaustion, locks, slow queries, replica lag, full storage, failed migration, unavailable backup, and restore validation through module 09.
For caches/search indexes, check warm-up, rebuild, stale/incorrect results, lost keys, memory eviction, source-of-truth reconciliation, and dependency overload during a cold start.

For object/file storage, check missing mount/bucket, permission expiry, full capacity, lifecycle mistakes, orphan objects, corrupt/partial upload, download failures, and separate metadata/content recovery.
For provider APIs, verify latency, rate limit, credential expiry, schema/error changes, quota depletion, partial outage, region failure, and ambiguous timeout using safe fixtures.
For webhooks, check delivery/retry/backlog age, signature/configuration failure, duplicate/out-of-order events, endpoint migration, dead letters, and controlled replay through module 14.
For email/SMS/push, distinguish requested, accepted, delivered where observable, bounced/rejected, delayed, and suppressed; verify destination cost, fan-out, preference, and retry-loop monitoring.
For payments/entitlements, detect paid-but-no-access, access-without-payment, renewal drift, pending refunds, duplicate effects, delayed callbacks, and reconciliation gaps through module 13.
For metered/credit products, detect reservation leaks, stale usage, reset errors, bill/product-unit mismatch, spend velocity, and failed/canceled work charged against policy through module 08.
For marketplaces/fulfillment, distinguish payment, stock/capacity, order acceptance, provider action, payout, cancellation, and actual fulfillment; monitor stranded intermediate states.

For AI/agent workloads, correlate model/provider/version, tool stages, latency, useful completion, refusals, quality signals, token/tool cost, retries, and continuation budget without unnecessary sensitive payload logging.

Test AI provider outage, model retirement/change, malformed output, retrieval gaps, context limits, slow streaming, runaway loops, and costly fallback; monitor user outcome and enforce scoped stops through modules 07-08.

For AI tool execution, distinguish generated intention from authorized action and confirmed effect; detect partial execution, unknown external outcomes, duplicate tools, failed cancellation, and missing human handoff.

For streaming/WebSocket/realtime services, monitor connection establishment, reconnect storms, dropped/late/duplicate updates, stale presence, fan-out, backpressure, draining, and partial stream failure.

For browser/mobile/desktop clients, monitor crashes, unhandled failures, release mapping, supported-version distribution, startup, deep-link failures, and API incompatibility with approved privacy handling.

For offline/background clients, check delayed telemetry, sync backlog, local/cloud conflicts, logout/account switch, stale credentials, storage exhaustion, and restored connectivity without duplicate effects.

For media/games/connected devices, check only applicable playback/session/pairing/telemetry/progression/update paths, stale device state, firmware/client compatibility, and user-visible continuity under disconnection.
Test monitoring backend unavailable during application failure; operators retain an adequate independent detection/diagnosis route and recognize evidence gaps.
Test primary paging/communication or identity outage during an incident; fallback access, contacts, documentation, and status updates remain usable.
Test certificate/domain expiry, DNS misconfiguration, incorrect system time, expired license, and billing suspension detection for applicable dependencies.
Test noisy neighbor, traffic spike, abuse burst, costly retries, and telemetry explosion using bounded fixtures; containment protects other tenants/services and useful recovery capacity.
Test data leak/credential compromise indicators and emergency revocation through specialist security review; audit trails and independent access remain available appropriately.
Test restore/rollback while old workers/schedulers/providers are still active; prevent duplicate execution, competing writers, and resurrection of retired resources.
Test long quiet periods followed by peak usage: expired credentials, cold caches, dormant schedulers, depleted credits, and untested response coverage are detected.
Test maintenance silence expiry, forgotten kill switch, stale canary metrics, and incorrect environment labels; operational tooling does not conceal an ongoing outage.
Test a nominally successful service that produces wrong/empty/stale results; correctness/freshness signals detect failure without relying on an exception rate.

For sensitive/public-service contexts, align critical availability, assisted access, data handling, incident communication, and qualified review with project-specific obligations; generic checklist completion does not establish compliance.

For internal tools or low-volume services, verify manual fallback, accountable working-hours response, stale-work detection, and staff continuity proportionately; absence of enterprise tooling alone is not a defect.

03 - Checkout, payment attempts, and security boundaries
04 - Events, idempotency, and financial state machines
08 - Refunds, disputes, reversals, and customer correction
09 - Invoices, approved tax configuration, and reconciliation
10 - Operations, migrations, and conditional commercial models
Payments and entitlements audit: start here
Official provider examples checked during authoring
Payments and entitlements audit - brief and report

values: Record product, release/configuration, environment, audit period/timezone, owner, decision needed, and evidence root; distinguish sandbox results from production evidence.

Inventory active plans, one-time purchases, subscriptions, trials, seats, metering, credits, discounts, invoices, refunds, disputes, payouts, and sales channels; exclude unsupported models with reasons.
Identify seller/merchant of record, payment processors, subscription/store platforms, connected accounts, currencies, settlement accounts, and responsibilities for each supported channel.

Record countries actually served, approved payment methods, customer types, tax treatment, invoice obligations, and reviewer-approved policies; do not assume a provider feature establishes obligations.
Map buyer, payer, account owner, beneficiary, billing admin, tenant admin, support, finance, and service-account roles; one person may not own all financial and access rights.
Inventory provider accounts, environment-specific credentials/secrets, prices/products, endpoints, subscribed events, API versions, schedulers, and manual billing actions.
Define sources of truth and relationships for checkout/order, payment attempt, authorization/capture, invoice, subscription, refund, dispute, credit, payout, and entitlement.
Define approved amount/currency/rounding rules, effective times, grace periods, cancellation/refund policies, credit expiry, and entitlement consequences before evaluating behavior.
Gather current checkout terms, pricing/help, contracts, consent/notice requirements, support policies, finance procedures, and incident records; surface contradictions.
Document external dependency and failure boundaries, including provider acknowledgement, asynchronous settlement, bank delays, delivery, reconciliation, and staff approvals.
Give each selected scenario reproducible preconditions, actor/tenant/plan, synthetic data, build/configuration, environment, timestamp/timezone, and method/tool/settings.
Capture expected and observed provider financial status, internal financial status, entitlement state, effective time, and side effects for each lifecycle scenario.
Distinguish source review, mocked fixtures, provider sandbox, deployed endpoint tests, and bounded production observation; do not claim one establishes another's correctness.
Verify persistent records and protected operations rather than relying on a success page, frontend badge, completed ticket, or callback response.
Record verified sample separately from potential affected customers/amounts/currencies; explain selection and estimation without summing unlike currencies as one amount.
Separate confirmed defects, verification gaps, policy ambiguities, and opportunities; unsupported financial models are not automatically missing requirements.
Deduplicate shared causes across payment, integration, reliability, security, product, and operations audits; retain all linked checks and one primary owner.
Assign defect severity, current exposure, confidence, delivery priority, and launch-blocker decision separately using realistic money/access/user impact.
Store redacted evidence with stable relative references and approved access/retention; exclude real card data, credentials, bank details, and unnecessary customer identifiers.
Reconcile selected statuses, exclusions, evidence gaps, findings, and owners; an unresolved critical boundary prevents a confident readiness conclusion.
Use synthetic identities and provider-approved sandbox/test methods; bound verification by target, rate, cost, duration, cleanup, and stop conditions without accidental real charges/refunds.
Select success, rejection, delayed/unknown outcome, duplicate/concurrent execution, cancellation, and recovery for every material money/access flow.
Cover relevant intersections such as cancellation during retry, role revocation during checkout, refund during dispute, quota expiry during a job, and restore after external payment succeeded.
Add incidents, provider-specific lifecycle cases, negotiated commitments, and market/channel-specific scenarios; expand coverage after inconsistent results.
Inventory versioned products/prices, currencies, intervals, quantities, eligibility, effective dates, and legacy mappings; identify the authoritative source and owner.
Derive payable product/price/currency and beneficiary account from trusted server-side rules; reject client-supplied amounts, unauthorized plan IDs, and tenant/customer substitution.
Verify disabled, archived, draft, expired, hidden, test, and other-channel prices cannot be purchased outside their approved eligibility.
Test zero, negative, fractional, minimum, maximum, and above-limit quantities according to product rules; billable seats/items are defined unambiguously.
Check per-unit, tiered, volume, graduated, minimum-commitment, package, and hybrid calculations only where offered, using approved worked examples.
Use integer minor units or an appropriate exact decimal representation for authoritative money, with documented conversion/precision boundaries rather than binary floating-point totals.
Verify supported currency exponents, amount limits, provider-specific charge/payout representations, and rounding rules against current exact-provider documentation.
Test line/subtotal/tax/discount/final rounding boundaries and aggregation order; displayed, authorized, captured, invoiced, refunded, and reported amounts reconcile.
Store amount and currency together; prohibit accidental currency substitution, cross-currency addition, and silent default currency changes.
Check localized currency symbols, decimal/grouping separators, units, billing interval, and tax-inclusive/exclusive presentation do not misrepresent the payable amount.
Test coupon/promotion validity, scope, effective time, redemption limit, first-purchase eligibility, and account/tenant binding using server-side decisions.
Check promotion stacking, usage retries, concurrent last redemption, invitation/referral loops, and canceled/failed purchase treatment against the approved rules.
Verify introductory prices, expiring discounts, free periods, renewal rates, and negotiated changes are shown and applied at the intended time.
Test legacy/grandfathered plans and migration opt-in/out where supported; current catalog updates do not silently rewrite existing commitments.
Verify custom agreements, annual prepayment, minimum quantities, purchase orders, sales-assisted quotes, and quote expiry through their own approved purchase/access path.
Check gift, referral, voucher, store-credit, and prepaid offers where present; distinguish promotional value from refundable customer payment and record restrictions.
Define whether credits cover tax, usage, renewals, add-ons, and upgrades; preview and final invoice apply the same allocation rules.
Test price changes while cart/quote/checkout is open; honor or refresh stale quotations according to explicit policy and require appropriate customer acknowledgement.
Verify currency changes, exchange-rate source/time, conversion fees, settlement presentation, and refund currency behavior where supported; disclose estimates versus locked amounts.
Verify shipping, service/platform fees, deposits, tips, surcharges, minimums, and optional add-ons only where offered; final totals reflect customer choices and approved disclosure.
Record approved tax/VAT registrations, served destinations, product classification, collection responsibilities, exemptions, and invoice treatment with reviewer/source references under module 11.
Test representative supported customer locations, business/consumer status, tax identifiers, exempt cases, and invalid/missing address against those approved configurations.
Check tax-inclusive/exclusive prices, discounted taxable base, shipping/fee treatment, rounding, refund adjustments, and effective-date changes against approved examples.
Verify before commitment the recurring amount or calculation, interval, trial conversion, renewal, cancellation, and relevant limitations are clearly presented on each supported checkout surface.
Verify required affirmative consent and terms/version evidence for the applicable transaction/channel; route exact wording, placement, timing, and retention to module 11.
Check localized, mobile, embedded, accessible, and provider-hosted experiences show consistent terms and totals; truncated layouts do not hide material conditions.
Compare marketing/pricing/help, sales quotes, checkout, portal, notices, and invoices with actual enabled products and access; identify materially false promises.
Verify trial/free labels distinguish no-cost use, card collection, authorization holds, future conversion, and usage charges according to the actual offer.
Check minimum term, pause/cancellation effect, early termination, refund eligibility, and remaining prepaid value are understandable and enforced only as approved.
Keep catalog/policy changes attributable, reviewed proportionately, effective-dated, recoverable, and traceable to affected existing/future customers.
Test unsupported destinations/currencies/payment combinations fail clearly before an unintended commitment or charge, without silently switching to another priced offer.
Reconcile sample calculations with provider sandbox results and approved finance examples; missing configuration or expertise remains a verification/policy gap.
Bind checkout/session/order to the authorized buyer, beneficiary account/tenant, catalog version, amount, currency, quantity, and environment using trusted server state.
Test unauthorized buyer/billing roles, another tenant's customer/session/order, changed membership, and suspended accounts through direct operations as well as UI.
Check guest checkout, sign-in during checkout, account creation, wrong signed-in identity, payer-versus-beneficiary, and invite acceptance only where supported.
Validate return/cancel destinations and portal links against approved routing; prevent attacker-controlled redirects and cross-account financial-session access.
Verify stale, expired, completed, reused, and another browser's sessions cannot create an unintended second purchase or attach it to the wrong customer.
Test double click, two tabs/devices, retry after timeout, refresh, and simultaneous checkout creation; documented idempotency prevents unintended duplicate commitments.
Scope operation identity to intended business action and parameters; reusing an idempotency key with another purchase/customer is rejected or handled explicitly.
Test failure before provider request, after provider acceptance, before local commit, and before response; discover actual provider state before creating a new payment.
Verify cart/price/discount/tax changes between session creation and completion obey the declared quote validity and authorization rules.
Separate test/live keys, catalogs, customers, callbacks, domains, and resources; inspect actual deployment bindings without exposing secrets.
Execute successful, declined, authentication-required, user-canceled, expired, and interrupted payment attempts for supported methods using provider fixtures.
Test browser back, closed tab, missing redirect, lost network, and app restart during authentication; recover status from authoritative state without false success/failure.
Distinguish pending, authorized, captured, settled, failed, and canceled statuses as relevant; do not equate authorization or asynchronous initiation with final collection.
For separate authorization/capture, test partial capture, repeated capture, expiry, cancellation/void, adjusted amount, and failed capture against provider-supported rules.
For delayed/bank/deferred methods, test late success/failure, expiry, cancellation availability, provisional access, and reversal according to the approved method policy.
For saved methods, verify customer ownership, explicit permitted use, default selection, replacement, removal, expiry, and subsequent off-session action handling.
Check wallets/local methods for supported device/browser/currency/market, fallback, authentication, and completion behavior; do not assume card semantics.
Verify payment-method update flow does not accidentally create a new purchase, clear arrears, or grant entitlements without the required authoritative outcome.
Verify receipts/order confirmations reflect actual state and amount; an accepted or pending payment is described truthfully.
Ensure a success redirect, client callback, forged session reference, or screenshot cannot independently mark payment paid or grant access.
Identify actual card/bank-data handling boundaries and qualified compliance ownership; verify prohibited data is absent from databases, logs, analytics, support tools, and AI prompts.
Keep privileged keys server-side, restrict provider/admin access, and verify safe errors, credential rotation, and environment-specific signing secrets through security review.
Check checkout/portal APIs, method-setup flows, payment-status lookups, and coupon checks for cross-tenant leaks, unauthorized changes, and enumeration.

Apply proportionate rate/abuse controls to checkout creation, failed attempts, card-testing patterns, promotion redemption, and expensive provider calls without blocking legitimate recovery/accessibility users.
Verify client scripts, embedded frames, payment-page configuration, CSP or equivalent controls, and change monitoring meet the project's reviewed collection model and obligations.
Prevent secrets and unnecessary payment/customer details in URLs, referrers, browser storage, error reports, test fixtures, and support exports.
Test supported checkout accessibility, localization, virtual keyboards, autofill, validation correction, and low-connectivity recovery without losing valid form context.
Define when stock/capacity, order fulfillment, entitlement, receipt, and usage allocation occur relative to authoritative payment state; partial steps have recovery paths.
Test payment success with local write/entitlement/delivery failure, and local order creation with payment failure; reconcile rather than silently losing paid value.
Check repeated provider payment attempts map to one intended order or subscription according to policy; failed attempts are not counted as additional purchases.
Test cancellation/expiry while payment is pending and a later success arrives; explicitly resolve money, fulfillment, access, and customer messaging.
Verify operators/customers can distinguish pending/unknown from confirmed failure and can locate a safe diagnostic reference without initiating another charge unnecessarily.
For live cutover, verify correct live endpoint, secrets, keys, price mappings, subscribed events, and safe rejection/receipt evidence without accidental real financial actions.
Retain full sandbox lifecycle evidence including final provider/internal/access state and effective time, with replay confirming no extra charge or access transition.
Inventory subscribed event types, endpoint/account/environment, payload/API versions, source objects, secrets, and business transitions they may trigger.
Verify provider authentication/signature with the required original bytes and metadata before state changes; reject absent/invalid/altered signatures through the actual ingress path.
Test wrong endpoint secret, test/live confusion, other provider/connected account, malformed payload, unsupported event version, and unexpected content type.
Apply provider-supported timestamp/replay checks with documented clock handling and secret rotation; valid delivery retries remain distinguishable from unauthorized replay.
Resolve provider customer/subscription/payment ownership to trusted internal records; untrusted event metadata does not create an arbitrary tenant entitlement.
Check changed/deleted customers, merged accounts, reused emails, stale membership, and connected-account scope; historical financial identity remains correctly bound.
Limit payload/work, isolate parsing errors, redact event evidence, and use least-privilege provider retrieval credentials through specialist security review.
Unknown/unsubscribed event types are handled according to documented policy without enabling a default privileged state transition.
Define durable receipt, acknowledgement semantics, processing state, retry ownership, and observable completion/failure according to the provider contract.
Test crash before receipt commit, after receipt commit, after acknowledgement, during business updates, and after effect but before completion marker.
Persist event identity and attempt/processing state so a duplicate is distinguishable from a previously received event whose business operation failed.
Test sequential and concurrent duplicate deliveries to multiple replicas; one intended business effect occurs without relying on process-local memory.
Check distinct event IDs describing the same underlying business effect; event-level deduplication alone does not create duplicate credits, refunds, or entitlement grants.
Scope deduplication keys to provider/account/environment and effect as needed; unrelated events with coincident identifiers are not suppressed.
Use appropriate transactions/constraints or a recoverable workflow for inbox, financial record, entitlement/outbox, and completion marker; partial commits can be repaired.
Test idempotent outbound operations with stable business identity and immutable relevant parameters; retry after an ambiguous timeout reconciles actual provider outcome.
Document provider idempotency scope, retention, parameter mismatch, error caching, and concurrent-request behavior; local durable identity covers longer business replay windows where needed.
Check deduplication/retention cleanup does not permit harmful late replay or erase evidence still needed for reconciliation and approved retention.
Define allowed transitions separately for order, payment, invoice, subscription, refund, dispute, credit, and entitlement; reject or reconcile impossible transitions.
Test reordered create/update/paid/failed/cancel/refund events, including tied timestamps; creation timestamp alone is not assumed to be a unique ordering/version key.
Retrieve or reconcile authoritative current state where required; stale events cannot overwrite a newer paid/canceled/refunded or otherwise authoritative state.
Check an event for one invoice/period/payment attempt does not incorrectly change another period's subscription or account access.
Test events arriving before dependent records exist; defer/reconcile safely rather than dropping accepted work or creating unbound financial objects.
Test delayed success after cancellation, failed payment after later recovery, refund after downgrade, and dispute after account deletion against explicit policies.
Distinguish event observation time, provider object version/state, billing period, effective entitlement time, and processing time in records and diagnosis.
Check subscription active/trial state, invoice paid, charge succeeded, and entitlement eligible are not treated as interchangeable without the defined commercial rule.
Verify concurrent webhook, scheduled reconciler, customer portal, support override, and API actions cannot reverse newer state or duplicate effects.
Bound retries, backoff, provider calls, queue size, and dead-letter handling; accepted but failed work is visible with an accountable repair route.
Detect missing events and stale subscriptions/invoices/entitlements via reconciliation/freshness rather than reliance on one timely callback.
Provide authorized audited replay with preview/scope/rate/cost limits; reprocessing uses current business rules/effective-time policy and preserves deduplication.
Test provider endpoint outage, WAF/proxy/body transformation, disabled event subscription, rotated secret, and delivery backlog through real deployed routing where safely authorized.
Migrate endpoint/API version/secret with explicit overlap and old/new worker behavior; both routes do not independently apply the same effect twice.
Verify replay after deployment/rollback/database restore does not forget already completed provider effects; reconcile against external authoritative records.
Correlate provider event/request/object IDs with internal operation and entitlement IDs without unnecessarily retaining full sensitive payloads.
Measure oldest unprocessed age, failures/retries, dead letters, reconciliation drift, and missing expected transitions; test alert receipt and support diagnosis.
Retain executed valid/invalid, duplicate/concurrent, reordered, missing, and crash-recovery evidence with final financial/access states, not only webhook response codes.
Define subscription identity, beneficiary, billing account, plan/version, interval, anchor/timezone, trial policy, and required authoritative outcome for activation.
Test no-card and card-required trials only where offered, including eligibility, verification, initial grants, end time, conversion amount, and permitted cancellation.

Check repeated signup, account merge, tenant switch, repeated trial, promotions, and manual trial extension against the declared eligibility rules without automatic penalties for legitimate shared users.
Test trial expiry with no payment method, failed method, authentication required, delayed callback, and scheduler outage; final access matches policy at the effective deadline.
Verify trial notices and conversion disclosures/consent for applicable markets/channels with qualified review under module 11; retain required evidence and detect delivery failure.
Verify incomplete/abandoned first purchase, pending invoice, delayed payment, and failed initial collection do not create an unintended indefinitely active subscription.
Test two simultaneous subscriptions/checkouts for the same intended account/product; supported multiple subscriptions are explicit and accidental duplicates are prevented/reconciled.
Check annual/monthly/custom terms, billing anchor changes, short/long first periods, leap dates, month-end, DST, and relevant timezone boundaries.
Test successful renewal with correct plan, quantity, tax, discount expiry, credits, period, and access; repeated events do not extend access twice.
Test failed/off-session/authentication-required renewal, method update, retries, and late success; users receive an accurate actionable state.
Define dunning cadence, retry ownership, grace duration, restriction, final expiry, and who can extend/reinstate; provider defaults do not silently define the product policy.
Verify grace access and quota/storage rules before/at/after cutoff, including direct APIs, cached sessions, active exports, and previously queued work.
Check failed delivery of payment-recovery notices, expired links, wrong billing recipient, account owner departure, and unavailable portal access; provide a supported recovery route.
Test payment recovery before and after final expiry, including several overdue invoices; reconcile which periods/obligations were paid and which access should return.
Verify canceling or removing a payment method does not automatically erase an existing amount owed or initiate an unintended new billing attempt contrary to policy.
Check price changes, expiring discounts, increased seats, changed usage rates, and annual renewal notices against approved effective dates and required notice/consent.
Reconcile invoice/payment state with subscription state so an old failed attempt cannot revoke access after a later authoritative recovery.
Test immediate versus scheduled upgrade/downgrade, preview, effective date, payment requirement, access transition, and unused-value treatment.
Verify proration rules for interval, price, seat, credit, and mid-period changes using approved examples; unpaid time is not credited or charged incorrectly.
Test failed/authentication-required upgrade payment and rollback/retention of prior access; do not silently grant unpaid premium capability or destroy paid baseline access.
Check downgrade below current seats/storage/usage, including grace, read-only, deletion/export, excess-member handling, and future work according to policy.
Test simultaneous plan/quantity changes, stale previews, repeated submissions, customer-portal updates, and support changes; resulting billing and access reconcile.
Verify pending/scheduled changes can be inspected, amended, or canceled as promised; old schedules do not override a newer accepted change.
Check adding/removing seats, invited/inactive members, minimum seat count, owner transfer, and billing-admin changes against the billable-seat definition.
Test add-on dependencies, multiple products/intervals, bundled allowances, and removal order where supported; access is not derived solely from a single plan string.
Verify currency, merchant/provider, store/channel, or legacy-plan transitions use an explicit supported migration path without duplicate renewal or lost paid time.
Test pause/resume collection versus pause/resume service only where supported; charges, entitlement, accumulated usage, and next period follow the distinct policy.
Verify immediate and period-end cancellation, effective time, last access date, remaining invoices, refunds, and queued changes against the accepted terms.
Test required online cancellation routes from all supported platforms, roles, locales, and failed-payment states; avoid unexplained dead ends or hidden extra commitments.
Check cancellation confirmation, renewal date removal/update, required acknowledgement, and notices reflect authoritative state even with delayed/missing callbacks.
Test cancellation during renewal, retry, pending upgrade, trial conversion, and an already initiated delayed payment; resolve final money/access/notice states explicitly.
Verify undo-cancellation/reactivation before period end and resubscription after expiry; prevent duplicate subscriptions, reset-abuse, or silent loss of promised remaining access.
Check account deletion versus subscription cancellation and payer/beneficiary separation; the user understands which financial obligations and retained records remain.
Verify canceled/expired access is enforced when webhook or scheduler fails through reconciler/freshness checks and direct protected-operation tests.
Test restoration of canceled/deleted customer records, provider reactivation, and database restore; old schedules and saved methods do not unexpectedly resume charging.
Verify manual subscription/trial overrides have explicit reason, scope, actor, effective/expiry time, review, and interaction with future automatic transitions.
Reconcile customer portal, UI, API, invoice, provider, notices, and support views for plan, period, cancellation, arrears, and future amount.
Execute full sandbox trial/renewal/failure/cancel/reactivation scenarios with final provider, internal financial, entitlement, and effective-time evidence plus safe event replay.
Inventory features, roles, products, plans, add-ons, seats, limits, flags, licenses, and entitlement sources; document the authoritative rule and beneficiary scope.
Define trial, pending, paid, grace, scheduled-cancel, expired, refunded, disputed, suspended, manual, and promotional eligibility separately where applicable.
Record entitlement start/end/effective time and timezone, source financial object, policy version, reason, actor, and superseding transition.
Define precedence among payment, trial, manual override, bundle, multiple subscriptions, organization membership, and suspension; conflicts have deterministic policy.
Distinguish payer, purchaser, assigned user, tenant owner, and current membership; purchase evidence alone does not authorize access to another tenant's resources.
Define read/create/edit/export/download/costly processing separately, including retained work after downgrade/expiry and permitted correction/export routes.
Verify grants and revocations are idempotent and attributable; one payment/event cannot extend a fixed license twice or duplicate an allowance.
Check legacy plans, custom contracts, grandfathered allowances, and add-on dependencies against explicit mappings rather than arbitrary display names.
Test allowed and denied direct server/API operations for protected features, not just hidden navigation or disabled buttons.
Enforce relevant entitlement on workers, scheduled tasks, exports/imports, batch/bulk actions, integrations, and costly provider calls.
Test another tenant/user/subscription/customer/license ID, stale role, suspended membership, and guest paths through the actual protected operations.
Verify client-controlled role/plan flags, local storage, unsigned metadata, success redirects, and arbitrary headers cannot grant paid access.
Check caches, JWT/session claims, replicas, edge authorization, and client refresh do not retain access beyond the documented revocation window.
