Escalate active compromise/material exposure through the established incident process. Do not delay containment merely to complete an audit matrix; preserve evidence where doing so does not prolong harm.

Assign remediation owner, acceptance test, dependencies, deadline and rollback/recovery approach. Risk acceptance requires an accountable decision, residual exposure and expiry, not a changed Pass status.

Record ready / ready subject to recorded conditions / blocked / insufficient evidence for the audited scope. Bind it to the candidate and invalidate affected assurance after material code/config/policy/exposure changes.

Inventory authentication methods, identity providers and account linking across web/native/API/admin clients. Identify authoritative subject identifiers and prevent ambiguous email/display-name mapping.

For self-managed passwords, use a maintained authentication implementation and current suitable password hashing/configuration. Verify deployed storage, migration/rehash behavior and protection of reset/recovery credentials; do not invent a home-grown hash scheme.
Test signup and verification for valid formats, plus-addressed emails, duplicate/racing creation and normalization rules. Do not merge distinct identities through undocumented canonicalization.
Check login, signup and recovery responses/timing for material account enumeration. Balance consistent errors with usable legitimate recovery; verify logs/support do not reintroduce disclosure.
Exercise guessing/throttling, distributed attempts and lockout recovery with tiny synthetic limits. Prevent both unlimited guessing and easy deliberate lockout of legitimate accounts.

Verify reset/verification/magic-link tokens are appropriately generated, scoped, short-lived as policy requires and single-use where intended. Test replay, expiry, wrong account and simultaneous redemption.

Check password/email/phone changes and identity linking/unlinking require appropriate current authorization or reauthentication. Verify attacker-controlled accounts cannot take over an existing subject through matching unverified attributes.
Verify MFA enrollment, step-up, disablement, recovery codes, lost-device response and alternate support recovery. Protect high-impact actions without creating an easier recovery bypass.
Where passkeys or hardware-backed credentials are offered, verify intended origin/RP, enrollment ownership, credential removal and recovery behavior using the provider's supported implementation.

Test account suspension/deletion/reactivation for actual authentication and downstream access behavior. Retired users must not retain unintended sessions, API keys, pending invitations or background authority.
Verify session issuance, identifier rotation where needed, idle/absolute expiry and fixation protection. Record different policies for ordinary, privileged and machine sessions.

Test logout, all-session revocation, password reset and disabled-account behavior across devices, replicas, cached sessions and refresh tokens. Record actual revocation delay and any bounded exceptions.

For session cookies, verify Secure, HttpOnly, appropriate SameSite, host/domain/path scope and expiration. Choose attributes that preserve required SSO/payment flows while maintaining the intended boundary.

Verify state-changing cookie-authenticated requests have effective CSRF protection. Check origin/token validation, content types, browser cross-site behavior and alternate methods; SameSite alone is not universal assurance.

Validate bearer/JWT tokens with trusted issuer, audience, signature/algorithm policy, expiry and key source. Do not accept arbitrary token-supplied verification keys or trust decoded claims without validation.
Check signing-key rotation, unknown key IDs, stale JWKS/caches, clock skew and provider outage behavior. A verification error must not enable an authentication bypass.

Scope access/refresh/API tokens by purpose, audience, environment and permission. Inspect browser storage, URLs, logs and crash telemetry for token leakage; native clients need appropriate secure storage.
Test refresh reuse/rotation/revocation behavior according to the chosen protocol and implementation. Include parallel refresh and stolen/old credentials without exposing real tokens in evidence.
Verify OAuth/OIDC flow configuration, redirect allowlists, state/nonce and PKCE where required by the selected flow/client. Test login return URLs using URL parsing rather than prefix matching.

Test external-origin, protocol-relative, encoded and authority-confusion return URLs with controlled destinations. Approved local/partner navigation must remain usable without enabling open redirects or token disclosure.
For SSO/SAML, verify signed-response/assertion handling, audience/recipient, time/replay constraints and tenant binding through maintained libraries. Do not trust unverified domain/group claims.

Check role/group mappings, invitation acceptance, just-in-time provisioning and account linking across organizations. A user in one enterprise must not gain another tenant's membership through a shared email suffix or stale invitation.
For SCIM/provisioning/offboarding, verify authenticated scoped requests, group/role updates, deactivation and downstream session/token/job revocation within the agreed window.
Verify emergency/recovery access cannot defeat required enterprise restrictions or create permanent unmonitored superuser credentials. Record owner, audit and review of exceptions.
Classify every material operation as public, authenticated, service-only or administrative. Enforce policy server-side for APIs, server actions, workers, WebSockets, exports, search and storage.
Derive user, tenant, ownership and role from trusted context. Reject client-controlled role/admin/owner fields and mass assignment in profile, team, object-create and direct database paths.
With synthetic A/B tenants, replace IDs in read/create/update/delete/list/search/export/share requests, including nested parent/child IDs. Verify absence of forbidden records and side effects.

Verify field-level authorization for sensitive attributes, bulk operations, related objects, counts and existence checks. Filtering the main object alone may still disclose membership, secrets or private metadata.

Enforce permission changes, member removal, team/project moves and plan expiry across cached sessions, workers and queued work. State whether accepted work completes and how remaining liability is contained.
Check role inheritance, multi-membership, invitation/ownership transfer and last-owner/admin removal. Prevent accidental privilege growth or an unrecoverable tenant with no accountable owner.

Test intentional sharing/public links for scope, recipient requirements, expiry, revocation and download/derived-object behavior. Document remaining access from already issued bearer links or cached copies.
Verify least-privilege service identities, scheduled jobs and integration credentials. User initiation must not turn a privileged worker into a confused deputy for arbitrary tenant/resources.

For client-accessible database APIs, attempt bounded anonymous reads/writes using only the intentionally public client key and real public role. Separate intended public views/functions from private denial.

Where RLS is used, verify enabled policies and read/write/insert/update/delete checks for actual application roles. Inspect owners, privileged/service roles, views and functions that may bypass ordinary policy behavior.
Check pooled connection/session tenant context is set and reset safely across requests and jobs. Reused connections or elevated function execution must not inherit another tenant's authority.

For database RPCs, stored procedures and security-definer code, verify execution grants, tenant checks and relevant name-resolution/privilege settings. A protected table does not automatically protect every callable function.

Keep sensitive object stores private by default and validate access before generating signed upload/download links. Test cross-tenant keys, overwrite, completion callbacks, expiry and unintended broad prefixes.
Verify authorization for search/vector indexes, analytics queries, replicas and derived exports. Copying data from the primary store must not lose its tenant or deletion boundary.
Require appropriate step-up/MFA and scoped authority for consequential admin operations, grants, exports, key access and security-setting changes. Test alternate APIs and bulk paths directly.

Where support impersonation exists, require explicit permitted scope, visible operator context, bounded sessions and a protected record of actor, target, reason and actions. Prevent silent permanent takeover.
Verify demo, support, break-glass and migration flows preserve material tenant/security boundaries. Exceptions require accountable ownership and expiry rather than an undocumented production bypass.

Execute relevant revocation, tenant substitution, anonymous/RLS, replay and support cases from [09](09-VERIFICATION-SCENARIOS-AND-EVIDENCE.md). Record the exact application role and persisted/provider effects.
Validate schema/types, size, range, length, encoding, IDs and business constraints on the server before consequential work. Client validation improves usability but does not establish trust.
Allowlist writable properties for each role/operation and reject unexpected privilege, ownership and billing fields. Test nested objects and bulk endpoints, not only individual profile forms.
Use parameterized database queries and safe query-building APIs. Check dynamic identifiers/order/filter expressions and NoSQL/operator inputs that may fall outside parameter binding.

Avoid evaluating untrusted code/templates or constructing shell commands from input. Use safe process APIs and constrained executable/argument choices; include filenames, job options and admin tooling.

Verify path normalization and allowed-root enforcement for reads/writes/deletes, archives and exports. Include encoded paths, symlinks where relevant and cross-platform separator assumptions with safe fixtures.

Inspect unsafe deserialization, XML external entity resolution and parser features according to the stack. Disable unnecessary capabilities and bound parsing without testing against real internal services.

Prevent prototype-pollution paths in recursive merge, property assignment and configuration handling. Reject dangerous keys where appropriate; deep copying alone is not a sanitizer or authorization policy.
Encode output for its actual HTML/text/attribute/URL/JavaScript/CSS context. Prefer safe text APIs when markup is unnecessary; URL allowlists and encoding address different hazards.

Sanitize intentionally supported rich HTML with a maintained configuration. Cover Markdown, user profiles, imports, generated content, email previews and admin/support views; later unsafe mutation can undo sanitization.
Use a harmless isolated rendered probe to verify stored/reflected/DOM content stays inert on relevant paths. Inspect execution/DOM and effects, not merely that the server saved a string.
Bound expensive validation, regex, parsing, decompression, nesting and result expansion. Include malformed requests and failure paths that can exhaust CPU/memory before ordinary rate controls act.

Handle CSV/spreadsheet exports, PDFs, email headers and logs using destination-specific safety rules. Untrusted formulas, markup or control characters must not become commands or misleading audit records.

Verify effective HTTP CSP and its actual enforcement/report-only state on important routes. Inventory script/style/connect/frame/worker/media dependencies and avoid a copied policy that silently allows the dangerous behavior.

Where nonce-based CSP is used, generate unpredictable per-response nonces and bind them to authorized markup. Inspect cache/CDN transformations and avoid treating a literal example nonce as a production secret/control.

Set appropriate frame-ancestors, base-uri and form-action explicitly where needed; they are not all covered by default-src. Deliver framing protection through a supported HTTP policy and test intended embedding.

Assess unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval, broad origins, JSONP-like endpoints and user-controlled same-origin content against CSP effectiveness. Preserve required flows while addressing executable content sources.

Where supported and justified, stage Trusted Types reporting, then verify enforcement and narrow policy creation. Audit policy sanitization; pass-through/default policies and unsupported browsers must not become the only XSS defense.

For DOMPurify/Trusted Types integration, verify options and return types against the installed version and sink usage. Review policy callbacks rather than copying the baseline's typed-return example unchanged.

Use SRI/version pinning where feasible for stable external scripts/styles and verify cross-origin CORS requirements. For dynamically changing vendors, record an alternative trust/update control instead of an unusable universal hash rule.

Inventory third-party scripts, tag managers, polyfills and widgets, their administrators and data access. Self-host/vet/pin where appropriate and test failure or compromise containment within the threat model.
Verify appropriate nosniff, Referrer-Policy, framing and cache headers across edge/origin/error routes. Do not equate a header-scanner grade with authorization or data-safety assurance.

Deliver Permissions-Policy as an HTTP header, with deliberate iframe delegation where needed. Test actual camera/microphone/location use and denial; a meta http-equiv example is not equivalent policy delivery.

Configure CORS for intended origins/credentials and inspect preflight plus actual responses. Broad access may be valid for public unauthenticated resources; CORS does not authenticate non-browser requests.
Test sensitive cookie-authenticated actions against CSRF and relevant cross-origin behavior. Verify downloads, redirects and alternate content types do not create a state-changing bypass.
Validate postMessage origin, source and message schema using controlled windows/frames. Avoid wildcard trust or interpreting untrusted messages as privileged commands.

Check browser storage, service workers, offline caches, history/URLs and tab/shared-device behavior for sensitive persistence and account switching. Client logout must not leave another user access to private cached content.

After synthetic A requests private content, repeat as B and anonymously through the actual CDN/cache path. Verify cache keys, headers and behavior prevent cross-identity reuse, including error and redirect responses.
Inventory URL-fetch, unfurl, import, screenshot, webhook-test, conversion and agent-tool fetchers. Define permitted schemes, hosts, ports and destination classes according to actual product needs.

Reject unintended loopback/private/link-local/metadata/internal destinations after parsing and resolution. Include IPv4/IPv6 and address forms supported by the runtime; verify through mocks or owned local fixtures.
Revalidate redirect destinations and address-resolution changes at the effective connection boundary. Include proxy/egress routing and prevent leaking credentials across redirected origins.
Bound outbound duration, redirects, response size, concurrency and content processing. Apply network/egress defenses where feasible without relying solely on a URL-string blacklist.

Authenticate incoming callbacks before privileged processing using the provider's intended signature/token mechanism. Test duplicate/replayed/out-of-order events and enforce tenant/operation scope independently.
Validate outbound webhook destination ownership and scoped secrets where needed, protect delivery logs and bound retries. A user-configured integration must not expose arbitrary internal endpoints.
Enforce upload count/bytes, allowed content, names, destination and processing policy server-side. Inspect actual content/metadata rather than trusting extension or client MIME alone.

Store untrusted files outside executable application paths and serve them with suitable content types/disposition/isolation. Review active HTML/SVG/documents according to permitted features and origin trust.

Authorize upload initiation, multipart completion, download, overwrite and deletion against actual tenant/object ownership. Constrain signed URLs and credentials by scope/expiry/platform capabilities.

Bound archive expansion, nesting, file count, media dimensions/duration and conversion work using small safe fixtures. Prevent traversal and resource exhaustion before durable writes or expensive processing.
Where scanning/content disarm is warranted, isolate/quarantine until the verdict and define unavailable/timeout behavior. A scanner result does not replace authorization or safe rendering.
Clean abandoned uploads, rejected files and failed derivatives under retention/recovery rules. Ensure processing errors do not leak paths, payloads or provider credentials.

Apply authorization and work-weight/complexity limits to GraphQL aliases/nesting, batch APIs, search, pagination, exports and bulk actions. One request may contain many expensive or privileged operations.
Authenticate/authorize WebSocket handshakes, subscriptions and individual consequential messages. Check origin, tenant changes, token expiry/revocation, reconnect and message-size/rate behavior.
Check API versions, route aliases, methods, content types and edge/origin parsing differences for bypassed controls. Use bounded owned fixtures for proxy/request-parsing assessments.

For native/desktop/mobile clients, validate deep links, IPC/plugin messages, update sources and local permissions relevant to the product. Client attestation or hidden endpoints do not replace server authorization.

Treat AI output, retrieved documents and tool responses as untrusted at rendering/action boundaries. Tool permissions and sensitive action authorization must remain independent of generated instructions.
Execute applicable browser, upload, injection, fetch, cache and API scenarios from [09](09-VERIFICATION-SCENARIOS-AND-EVIDENCE.md). Record allowed flows as well as denial and downstream effects.

Map personal/sensitive data through forms, clients, APIs, databases, files, search/vector stores, analytics, logs, support, vendors and backups. Include identifiers, inferred attributes and derived outputs, not just explicit profile fields.

Record purpose, accountable owner, collection source, necessity, recipients, access, region, retention and applicable commitments for each material data category. Flag unknown-purpose fields and unused exports/datasets.
Minimize collection, precision, default visibility and retention to product needs. Examine hidden form fields, auto-collected SDK data, URLs, device IDs and unnecessary third-party enrichment.

Verify privacy notices, user settings and product claims reflect actual flows and provider configuration. Compare runtime requests and stored data with reviewed disclosures, not only a policy-page checklist.

Identify high-impact/sensitive use cases, vulnerable populations, children or special contractual restrictions for accountable assessment. Define product scope/exclusions and tailored review without assuming a universal age or legal threshold.

Distinguish anonymization from pseudonymization and reversible identifiers. Document linkage/reidentification risks and access to lookup tables; hashing an email does not automatically make it anonymous.

Restrict personal data in public profiles, shared links, directories, search snippets and notifications. Test default visibility, previews, counts and account-discovery behavior with synthetic identities.

Review production-data use in development, QA, demos, screenshots, issue trackers and AI assistance. Prefer synthetic/minimized fixtures and control any justified copies with access, retention and deletion ownership.
Inventory cookies, local/session storage, pixels, beacons, analytics, replay, advertising, attribution and tag-manager rules across pages, clients and authenticated states.

Classify essential and optional processing with the project's reviewer. Where consent or another specific user choice is required, verify the actual pre-choice behavior and vendor calls, not merely a banner's presence.
Test accept/reject/selective choice, withdrawal, expiry and cross-device/account behavior against documented rules. Prevent a tag-manager, embedded widget or server-side relay bypassing the choice.
Keep collection/preferences coherent across login, logout, account switching, new SDK versions, locale and mobile/native clients. Do not silently merge unrelated users' identities or settings.
Request location/camera/microphone/contact/notification permissions in context with understandable purpose. Handle denial/revocation and avoid collecting or retaining more precise data than needed.
Verify device/iframe capabilities through effective Permissions-Policy and platform permissions. Permission to access a device feature is separate from permission to transmit or retain its data.
Inspect fingerprinting, persistent IDs, cross-site links and server-side tracking/enrichment against disclosed scope and reviewed requirements. Removing one cookie does not prove tracking stopped.

Inspect actual analytics/error/replay payloads using synthetic secrets and personal fields in forms, DOM text, URLs, chat, dynamic components and network capture. Mask/exclude before transmission, not only in the vendor UI.
Test replay masking on late-loaded fields, rich editors, attachments and account-switch states. Verify failure/default configuration does not record passwords, payment data or prohibited content.

Verify consent-required capture/transmission stops before choice and after rejection/withdrawal, including buffer flushes, retries, tag-manager and server-side paths. Document any justified essential telemetry separately.
Bound telemetry retention/cardinality, recipients and staff access. Check downloadable recordings, shared dashboards, support links and vendor administrator roles.

Review emails/SMS/push notifications, receipts and support messages for sensitive content, lock-screen exposure, wrong recipients, reply threading and tenant context. Use approved synthetic recipients in tests.
Restrict exports, reports, attachments and customer-support data to the appropriate operator/tenant. Check signed-link lifetime, logs, cached copies and external sharing defaults.
Record processors/subprocessors, purpose, data sent, hosting/processing regions, retention, deletion capability, contractual/security commitments and accountable vendor owner.

Verify actual provider account/settings and SDK defaults for training/reuse, logging, retention and regional routing where material. A marketing statement or another plan's guarantee is not evidence for this account.

Check data transferred through middleware, proxies, integrations, backup providers and support tools. Include fallback providers and failover regions so outage behavior does not silently alter approved data flows.
For AI features, inspect prompts, attachments, chat history, memory, embeddings, retrieval snippets, tool inputs/outputs and evaluation datasets for necessary scope and tenant isolation.

Treat embeddings, summaries, derived profiles and model/provider logs as potentially sensitive where linkable. Define export/deletion/retention effects and avoid assuming deleting the source removes all derived data.
Verify vendor offboarding, access revocation, data export/deletion and residual-retention confirmation under actual commitments. Distinguish a sent request from completed erasure.
Define supported privacy/account requests, identity verification, authorized-agent handling where applicable, scope, ownership and required response timelines with accountable review.
Test self-service/admin export as the legitimate synthetic subject and another tenant. Include relevant messages, files, settings and derived categories without exposing secrets or other users' data.
Protect export generation, download, expiry and delivery channels. Avoid an unauthenticated permanent archive or a background job that runs with the wrong tenant authority.
Test correction/deletion across active databases, object stores, indexes, caches, analytics, integrations and vendors. Record eventual processing and failures with retry/reconciliation ownership.

Where soft deletion is used, verify ordinary reads/search/exports/RLS and unique-key/recreation behavior hide or handle retired records as intended. Soft deletion alone does not fulfill an erasure promise.
On account deletion/offboarding, revoke sessions, refresh/API tokens, shares, integrations and pending work as policy requires. Protect shared/organization-owned data and explain retained records.
Test duplicate, concurrent and interrupted export/delete requests plus late provider callbacks. Prevent re-created records, unbounded retries and a race that restores access after deletion.

Verify privacy requests cannot be abused for account takeover, cross-tenant deletion, insider access or unauthorized disclosure. Support recovery must not be an easier path than normal identity checks.

Define retention/deletion schedules by data category and system with justified exceptions, legal holds and accountable owners. Verify actual lifecycle tasks and vendor settings rather than policy text alone.

Check backups, replicas, object versions, logs and disaster-recovery copies for access and bounded expiry. Document why immediate removal may differ from active-store deletion under reviewed commitments.

Prevent restored backups, replayed imports or delayed sync from silently resurrecting deleted users/data contrary to policy. Maintain a proportionate reconciliation/deletion mechanism for restored state.
Verify encryption/access control for retained sensitive stores and exports, including key recovery and authorized use. Encryption does not remove purpose, access or retention responsibilities.
Record evidence of actual completion, justified retention and unresolved vendor/backup expiry. Assign an owner/date to delayed confirmation; a UI success message is not proof of system-wide erasure.
Reassess data flows after new SDKs/providers, regions, AI features, collection fields, user populations or product purposes. Update notices/settings/reviews before relying on earlier assurance.
Execute applicable consent, replay-payload, export/delete, vendor and restore cases from [09](09-VERIFICATION-SCENARIOS-AND-EVIDENCE.md). Keep sanitized evidence separate from real personal data.

Inventory privileged API/database/payment/signing/AI credentials, OAuth refresh tokens, SSH/deploy keys, webhook secrets and recovery material. Record owner, consumers, environment, privilege, rotation and revocation route without copying values.
Inspect current source, relevant history, real environment files, examples, built frontend assets, source maps, CI artifacts, package archives and container layers for secret exposure.

Inspect logs, errors, monitoring/replay, support exports, screenshots, AI chats and agent/tool artifacts for credentials or unnecessary sensitive payloads. Review artifacts outside the repository as part of scope.

Keep intentionally public client keys separate from privileged secrets and verify their associated roles. A public key is safe only within an enforced permission design, not because it is labeled public.
Verify real environment/secret files are excluded from new commits and placeholders contain no working credentials. Ignoring a file does not remove an existing historical exposure.

Revoke/rotate exposed credentials, update all consumers and confirm the old credential is ineffective through safe verification. Deleting a file/commit, rewriting history or hiding a source map does not invalidate a stolen key.
Scope service secrets per environment/project/role and restrict who can read, issue, rotate, revoke and recover them. Check shared accounts and long-lived keys for excessive blast radius.

Use appropriate secret storage/injection rather than distributing secrets in clients, images or downloadable configuration. Verify permissions on temporary files, process/environment exposure and CI output.
Ensure missing required production secrets fail safely, with no fallback signing/password keys, debug bypass or accidental live/test provider substitution.
Rehearse proportionate rotation/revocation with scoped fixtures, including queued jobs, cached connections and rollout overlap. Document how emergency revocation affects service and recovery.

Use maintained platform/library cryptography appropriate to the data and protocol; avoid custom algorithms, static nonces/IVs and embedded master keys. Verify implementation-specific configuration with current primary guidance.

Verify encryption in transit and at rest for sensitive databases/files/backups and long-lived credentials where required by the threat model. Record actual provider settings, key ownership and trust boundary.

Separate encrypted data from unnecessary key access; restrict decrypt/export/admin privileges and protect audit records. Disk encryption alone does not isolate authorized application roles or compromised accounts.
Verify key generation, versioning, rotation, recovery and destruction against data lifetime. Test old/new key readability and recovery without destroying the sole usable key or production copy.

Identify risks from URL/bearer tokens, signatures, hashes and pseudonymous IDs. Do not treat encoding/hashing as encryption or assume secrets remain safe merely because the database disk is encrypted.
Bind release artifacts to source/build/runtime/configuration and verify deployed versions. Inspect application packages, base images, OS/runtime components, plugins, SDKs and client-bundled code.

Run suitable dependency/image/security checks with recorded tool/database dates and scope. Triage affected versions, reachability and exposure; a scanner's empty output or severity score is incomplete assurance.

Verify maintained/supported dependencies and update ownership. Evaluate fixes using compatibility/relevant tests; do not run automatic dependency upgrades merely because the baseline lists an audit-fix command.

Review lockfiles, registry/source selection, install/build hooks, downloaded binaries and dependency-confusion/typosquatting risks where applicable. Protect publishing and organization/package ownership.

Protect CI/workflow definitions, runners, caches and artifacts from untrusted contribution execution or privilege escalation. Scope workflow tokens and production secrets; inspect alternate/manual release paths.

Verify promotion/signing/update verification appropriate to distributed packages and containers. Mutable tags, public download links or an unsigned manifest must not silently replace the reviewed release.
Inventory third-party JS/CSS/polyfills and tag-manager changes alongside backend dependencies. Record version/integrity/trust/update controls and administrators who can inject code into production.

Review production source-map policy and actual reachability on CDN/origin/build artifacts. Hidden maps can still be served; restrict sensitive original sources/secrets while retaining approved debugging capability.
Check artifact retention, access and cleanup for secrets and personal data. Include old releases, failed builds, preview bundles, caches and deleted-branch environments.

Verify TLS/certificates, redirects, renewal and intended upstream encryption for actual domains, callbacks, APIs, database connections and management interfaces. Inspect mixed content and insecure failover paths.
Enable HSTS only after required HTTPS coverage and recovery implications are verified. includeSubDomains and preload need separate domain-wide review; copied values are not universally appropriate.
Restrict exposed ports, database/cache/admin consoles, debug endpoints and management APIs. Check previews, old deployments, origin IPs and alternate IPv4/IPv6 routes within permitted scope.
Verify trusted proxy hops, forwarded identity/host/scheme handling, allowed hosts and edge/origin rules. Untrusted headers must not grant internal trust, bypass limits or poison links/caches.

Verify runtime/container privileges, user identity, mounts, filesystem access, service isolation and resource limits against actual application needs. A non-root image alone does not prove host isolation.
Check remote administration, SSH/access gateways, firewall/egress controls and provider dashboard MFA/recovery. Preserve a separately controlled emergency access path with accountable ownership.

Isolate production/staging/local credentials, provider callbacks, data and networks where required. Verify tests/previews cannot write real customer data, send unintended messages or invoke production privileges.
Validate effective feature flags, safe defaults, diagnostics and security configuration after clean install, restart, deploy, rollback and failover. Record drift from code-defined intent.

Protect backups/snapshots/configuration exports and recovery accounts with appropriate access, retention and off-host availability. Verify restore can recover required keys without exposing them to ordinary users.
Check restore/rollback cannot reintroduce exposed keys, permissive policies, deleted-account access or outdated vulnerable artifacts. Reconcile old credentials and security state explicitly.

Confirm organization-controlled domain/repository/provider ownership, billing/recovery contacts, primary/backup administrators and patch responsibilities. Avoid a sole recovery path tied to one person's device or memory.

Execute applicable secret, artifact, transport, source-map, configuration and recovery scenarios from [09](09-VERIFICATION-SCENARIOS-AND-EVIDENCE.md). Retain sanitized proof of old-key rejection and deployed state where claimed.
Define material audit events: authentication/recovery, role/tenant changes, admin/support access, credential changes, exports/deletes, policy/config changes and consequential denied attempts.

Where sensitivity/commitments require read auditing, capture important record reads as well as writes. Record trusted actor/service, tenant, target, operation, outcome, time and correlation without unnecessary payloads.
Protect event integrity, access and retention. Restrict deletion/alteration, prevent untrusted text from forging events and retain appropriate time synchronization and correlation across services.
Verify logs/errors/traces do not expose credentials, session tokens, personal payloads or private queries. Test redaction with synthetic markers before transmission and inspect real telemetry paths.

Detect meaningful account/privilege changes, unusual exports, repeated boundary violations, suspicious credential use and relevant data/vendor access. Choose signals based on actual exposure and operator capacity.

Exercise controlled relevant alerts through actual delivery, acknowledgement and escalation. Record accountable recipients, response availability and an accessible runbook; configuration alone is not receipt evidence.

Bound event/alert volume, key cardinality, retention and ingestion cost during abuse. Preserve useful aggregated evidence while preventing security monitoring from becoming an availability/spend problem.
Restrict observability, support/replay and audit-dashboard access by role/tenant. Check shared links, downloadable exports, vendor staff access and offboarding of former responders.
Review actual user/service/admin/provider access at an agreed risk-based cadence and after important personnel/architecture changes. Record reviewer, date, exceptions and completed revocations.
Verify offboarding removes sessions, keys, group membership, provider consoles, repositories, support tools and downstream integrations within the agreed window. Check dormant and emergency accounts.

Maintain a vulnerability disclosure/contact and triage route appropriate to the product. Test accountable receipt with a synthetic harmless report; do not solicit or perform unauthorized third-party testing.
Track security advisories, dependency/runtime/provider changes and patch ownership. Define severity/response based on affected scope, business exposure and relevant commitments.

Commission scoped independent testing where risk/commitments warrant it. Record scope, permission, exclusions and final-revision applicability rather than treating an old penetration-test label as blanket assurance.

Track remediation with owner, acceptance criteria, deadline and focused retest. Preserve original findings and root-cause reasoning; suppressions/risk exceptions need rationale, accountability and expiry.

Review security-relevant changes independently through the established process. Verify effective review/gate execution on the final revision; installing a review plugin does not establish that a review happened.
Assign incident lead, technical responder, privacy/legal reviewer and communication duties proportionate to team size. Record primary/backup availability, authority and emergency contacts.
Keep runbooks for exposed keys, account takeover, cross-tenant access, sensitive telemetry, malicious files, provider compromise and data loss relevant to the system.
Ensure runbooks, recovery references and incident communication remain accessible during host/app/provider failure. Rehearse authorized emergency access without printing credentials in evidence.

Verify scoped containment: revoke keys/sessions, disable vulnerable features, suspend accounts, block unsafe egress, pause queues and stop costly tools. Include retries, child tasks and old deployments.

Record residual exposure from already downloaded data, cached content, signed links, uncancellable remote work and delayed revocation. A kill switch cannot retract every earlier disclosure or external action.

Preserve relevant redacted evidence, timeline, affected versions, identities and provider records while avoiding unnecessary duplication of sensitive material. Do not let evidence collection delay urgent containment.

Assess actual/potential data, integrity, availability and financial impact with explicit unknowns. Distinguish confirmed access from possible exposure and use accountable review for notification/contractual duties.

Prepare internal/customer/vendor communication and support handling as appropriate. Any actual messages follow task authorization and the established incident process; the audit itself does not send them.

Verify recovery restores safe permissions, current keys, deletion/offboarding state and data integrity. Prevent rollback or restore from reactivating compromised access or replaying forbidden effects.
Restore service gradually after containment with monitored limits and known-good state. Define re-engagement conditions for stops and check delayed retries/callbacks cannot reopen the exposure.
Reconcile vendor copies, exposed credentials, customer requests and incomplete cleanup. Assign owner/date to delayed confirmation instead of claiming complete eradication from code changes alone.
Capture lessons and verified corrective actions after material incidents. Track recurring root causes and procedure failures, not merely a completed postmortem document.

Bind release/security decisions to code, artifact, runtime/config/policies, exposure and evidence time. Unverified critical controls and material active exposure may prevent a confident release decision.

Reassess after new features, data categories, AI tools, vendors, regions, roles and client platforms. Review expired exceptions and inherited infrastructure evidence before carrying assurance forward.

Execute applicable audit, alert, offboarding, containment/restore and regression cases from [09](09-VERIFICATION-SCENARIOS-AND-EVIDENCE.md). Record residual gaps, accepted risk and operational handoff explicitly.

vulnerabilities. Use a strict CSP + Trusted Types (below) instead.

headings.text: VPS, Coolify, DNS, and network audit library
Audit VPS Coolify DNS and network protection

values: Record hosting account, instance IDs, regions, OS/kernel, CPU architecture, Docker, Coolify, proxy, DNS/CDN, and relevant versions/plans; distinguish installed, configured, and running state.
Identify physical/virtual hosts, control/build/remote servers, public/private IPv4 and IPv6, interfaces, VPNs, floating addresses, load balancers, and provider firewalls.
Map domains, registrar, authoritative DNS, delegated subzones, certificates, proxy routes, mail providers, and application/administrative hostnames to owners.
Inventory applications, listeners, published container ports, private services, workers, schedules, volumes, databases, object stores, and externally configured triggers.
Identify critical journeys, sensitive data, tenant/project boundaries, allowable downtime/data loss, restoration targets, capacity expectations, and budget.
Define provider/customer responsibilities and who owns OS, Docker, Coolify, proxy, application, DNS, backup, monitoring, and incident response in the actual service model.
Map privileged dependency chains across hosting, recovery email, registrar, DNS, identity, source control, registry, Coolify, servers, and backup accounts.
Name every application inheriting a shared control and what remains app-specific; separate shared-host risk from per-app authentication and authorization.
Record allowed target addresses/domains, methods, source networks, synthetic accounts, request/rate/time bounds, side effects, and stop conditions before live verification.
Separate read-only configuration review, ordinary bounded connection checks, restore rehearsals, access changes, and load/fault tests; authorization for one does not establish the others.
Capture expected allowed/denied paths for each exposed service, address family, ingress mode, and administrative source using the exposure matrix.
Distinguish provider configuration, host/container rules, actual listeners, external reachability, and application response; a screenshot of one layer does not verify the others.
Use a controlled allowed request alongside a denial check where feasible; a failed connection alone can reflect an outage, routing failure, or wrong destination.
Record timestamps/timezone, environment, resource/revision/version, source vantage point, tools/settings, exact target, observed result, and evidence limitations.
Sample each materially different host, firewall attachment, Docker network mode, proxy path, address family, record type, role, and persistent-data class; expand after inconsistent results.
Inspect actual deployed configuration and account capabilities rather than assuming upstream defaults or a guide written for another release apply.
Redact evidence and keep credential/key values out of reports; record secure custody references and demonstrated retrieval without displaying secrets.
Mark missing dashboard access, absent IPv6 vantage, unexecuted restore, unavailable provider telemetry, and uncertain external consumers Not verified with the required follow-up.
Assign each finding one root cause, primary module/owner, related check IDs, affected hosts/apps, severity, confidence, current exposure, priority, and blocker rationale.
Separate active exposure, latent enablement risk, verification gap, accepted limitation, and optional improvement; lack of a paid product is not itself a defect.
Propose the smallest effective fix with legitimate-traffic impact, lockout prevention, compatibility, dependencies, acceptance checks, and rollback/forward recovery.
Record accepted risk with accountable person, reason, compensating controls, expiry, and revisit trigger; acceptance does not turn an unmet control into Pass.
Recheck changed controls and directly affected apps after implementation; preserve actual results and unresolved gaps rather than marking planned mitigation verified.
Report selected/assessed/status counts with an explicit denominator and sample coverage; do not present a checklist completion percentage as a security guarantee.
Confirm accountable ownership of hosting, registrar, DNS, CDN, identity, source control, registry, billing, and backups; remove abandoned personal or former-contractor control.
Use available strong MFA and protect enrollment/recovery; verify that privileged account recovery cannot bypass the intended boundary through an insecure mailbox or shared credential.
Maintain off-host recovery methods, trusted contacts, alternate billing/renewal alerts, and emergency access independent of the failing VPS or hosted domain where practicable.
Review members, roles, service accounts, sessions, API keys, authorized OAuth apps, and last use; revoke obsolete access with consumer-aware sequencing.
Scope automation tokens to necessary accounts/resources/actions and supported expiry/IP constraints; give integrations separate identities so revocation is attributable and bounded.
Verify audit/change notifications reach a monitored recipient and that sensitive account, domain, and billing changes can be investigated.

Record provider support authentication, console/rescue access, identity verification, service suspension, and escalation procedures; do not rely on an unreachable dashboard as the only incident route.
Check renewal dates, payment failures, service limits, domain expiry, abuse contacts, and resource cancellation responsibilities; accidental suspension is an availability risk.
Inventory SSH users, keys/certificates, authorized-key sources, automation accounts, forwarding, jump hosts, listening addresses, and alternate administrative protocols.
Use attributable individual administrative access and protected private keys; distinguish interactive operators from unattended Coolify and backup automation.
Review effective SSH configuration including include files, Match blocks, cloud-init/provider changes, authentication methods, root access, and user restrictions rather than one edited file.
Verify a second working authorized session and provider console/rescue access before changing SSH authentication, listening ports, routing, or firewall sources; preserve a tested recovery path.
Limit administrative reachability to required operators/VPN/jump hosts and controller addresses; account for dynamic home IPs, remote controllers, and IPv6.
Review sudo, Docker-group/socket access, service-unit editing, writable privileged scripts, cron, and mount permissions as privilege paths; a non-root username may still have host-equivalent powers.
Check SSH host-key verification for operators and automation, especially after rebuild/IP reuse; investigate a changed fingerprint rather than disabling verification globally.
Restrict agent/TCP/X11 forwarding and tunneled access according to actual use; ensure a narrow SSH allowlist cannot still expose unintended internal services through an overly privileged account.
Revoke stale keys, shared credentials, rescue passwords, temporary users, and emergency access after use; check every relevant host and automation consumer.
Detect failed/suspicious authentication and unexpected privileged sessions; optional blocking tools require observed effectiveness and false-lockout recovery.
Verify OS/kernel/packages remain supported using actual versions and primary advisories; plan patches, reboots, maintenance windows, and urgent fixes with an owner.
Review package repositories, signing/trust configuration, third-party installers, unattended updates, and unsupported pinned packages for avoidable compromise or upgrade failures.
Inventory enabled services, systemd timers, cron, startup scripts, remote agents, shells, and unexpected privileged processes; remove obsolete components only after confirming purpose.
Check ownership/mode of secrets, environment files, SSH material, backup config, service files, sockets, and privileged executables; include inherited group and ACL access.
Review temporary directories, shared writable locations, symlink handling, and privileged scripts that process untrusted paths or filenames.
Verify time synchronization, timezone, hostname, local DNS, and certificate trust; clock drift can break authentication, TLS, schedules, and incident correlation.
Inspect disk bytes, inodes, mount health, filesystem errors, read-only remounts, swap/OOM behavior, and persistence of critical paths; capacity monitoring must cover the volume actually used.
Review host audit/auth/system logs, rotation, retention, off-host export, and privacy; diagnose without filling disk or recording secrets.
Check restart policies, service dependencies, boot ordering, and recovery after a real reboot where authorized; runtime state is not proof configuration survives restart.
Evaluate AppArmor/SELinux/seccomp and kernel controls supported by the installed stack; document necessary exceptions rather than blindly applying a generic sysctl/hardening script.
Confirm provider agents, guest tools, cloud-init, rescue images, and console functionality are understood and appropriately secured; provisioning metadata and credentials need explicit ownership.
Review access to instance metadata, local credential services, and private management endpoints from workloads; enforce applicable boundaries without breaking required platform operation.
Identify workloads that share a kernel, host account, filesystem, registry credential, backup identity, or control plane; document the resulting compromise blast radius.
Separate production and untrusted build/preview workloads where needed by trust level, not only by project labels or container names.
Document baseline provisioning, secure configuration sources, drift detection, and owner; avoid manual-only settings that disappear during host replacement.
Preserve required recovery/license/evidence assets while retiring obsolete accounts, daemons, keys, packages, and instances; verify dependencies and retained billing.

Treat suspected host compromise as a trust failure: plan isolation, evidence preservation, clean rebuild, and credential rotation from a trusted system rather than assuming a restart removes persistence.
Validate operator handover when the original maintainer is absent, including safe credential retrieval, console access, patching, and restoration ownership.
Inventory public/private interfaces, routes, listeners, provider firewalls, host rules, Docker mappings, reverse proxies, tunnels, and alternate direct paths on every host.
Confirm provider policies are active and attached to the correct instance/interfaces, with intended direction, protocol, source range, address family, and effective rule precedence.
Apply default-deny ingress where appropriate and justify every exception by consumer/owner; do not confuse a saved rule template with an attached effective policy.
Compare runtime and persistent firewall state; verify rules survive supported reboots, daemon restarts, deployments, and provider-side interface/IP changes.
Identify the actual iptables/nftables/backend integration and forwarding path before changing Docker rules; policies must match the installed engine/backend.
Verify Docker-published ports externally rather than assuming UFW's normal input policy covers their traffic; use a supported policy at the effective filtering layer.
Do not disable Docker firewall management without a complete supported replacement and validation; check container routing and intended isolation after network-policy changes.
Inspect wildcard/loopback/specific-address binds, Compose ports versus expose declarations, host networking, direct routing, and extra port mappings for unintended public paths.
Keep database, cache, Docker API/socket, registry administration, metrics, debug, development, and internal API listeners private unless a justified protected integration needs access.
Verify management access from allowed and disallowed sources, including Coolify controllers, backup agents, monitoring, and temporary maintenance paths.
Test IPv4 and IPv6 independently across provider rules, host rules, public binds, Docker publishing, DNS A/AAAA, and VPN routes; one passing family does not establish the other.
If IPv6 is intentionally unused, verify actual interfaces, routes, records, and exposure match that decision; deleting AAAA alone does not close an IPv6 listener.
Preserve necessary ICMP/ICMPv6 and path-MTU behavior according to the network design; blanket blocking can break diagnostics, neighbor discovery, or larger transfers.
Check TCP and UDP separately for services that use both, including DNS, VPN, game/media traffic, and HTTP/3 where enabled.
Review connection tracking capacity, established/related rules, fragment handling, asymmetrical routing, and rate rules where relevant; verify legitimate connections under the supported topology.
Check NAT/hairpin behavior, loopback exposure, public-to-private routing, and access from neighboring hosts/workloads; a public denial does not prove east-west isolation.
Validate MTU/MSS and encapsulation overhead for VPN/tunnel paths using bounded checks; investigate size-dependent or streaming failures rather than disabling TLS verification.
Record intended protection and recovery for floating/additional IPs, failover interfaces, load balancer health probes, and IP changes; ensure old policies do not become a bypass.
Map private/overlay networks, memberships, routes, ACLs, DNS search domains, exit nodes, and advertised subnets; private addressing alone is not authorization.
Restrict cross-project traffic to required flows and test denied paths where authorized; shared Docker/VPN membership may permit lateral access despite separate dashboard projects.
Scope VPN/device identities, admin rights, enrollment, expiry, revocation, and lost-device response; verify removal takes effect on active paths.
Check split/full tunnel behavior, DNS leakage, route conflicts, client-IP attribution, and management reachability during VPN/control-plane outage.
Inventory required egress for DNS, NTP, package/registry access, ACME, OAuth, payments, email, object storage, backups, and provider APIs.
Where egress restrictions are required, verify the effective outbound layer and actual allowed/denied traffic; do not infer outbound filtering from an inbound-only provider firewall.
Account for changing provider IPs/CDNs, DNS resolution, IPv6, TLS endpoints, and proxy exclusions in egress policy; avoid brittle IP lists without update ownership.
Review access to link-local metadata, host services, private control planes, and other tenants from untrusted workloads; pair network restriction with application SSRF controls.
Confirm DNS resolution and time sync have appropriate redundant/available paths and are not accidentally blocked during policy tightening.
Detect unexplained outbound traffic, scanning, mail, exfiltration, and bandwidth growth; identify the originating workload and response owner.
Do not expose inbound DNS merely to permit outbound lookups; deliberate DNS hosting needs explicit authoritative/resolver role, recursion policy, transfer access, and amplification review.
For mail hosting, inventory protocol/port exposure, authentication, relay policy, provider restrictions, reverse DNS, abuse handling, and availability separately from the web proxy.
For game/voice/media/VPN services, verify required UDP/TCP ranges, identity, per-protocol limits, upstream mitigation, and client compatibility; ordinary HTTP WAF rules may not apply.
For intentionally external databases or replication, require justified clients, narrow sources, authentication, encryption/identity validation, monitoring, and revocation/recovery procedures.
Check public container registries, artifact servers, object gateways, and management agents for anonymous write/admin routes and direct-port bypasses.
Use ordinary bounded connection/application checks from authorized external vantage points; record source, destination, family, protocol, expected result, and actual response.
Pair denied tests with allowed service checks and confirm the intended origin, not a cached edge response or a different instance, was observed.
Revalidate exposure after deploying a new service, publishing ports, switching Docker backend, enabling IPv6, adding a tunnel, or replacing a firewall policy.
Inventory Coolify instance/version, control-plane host, remote servers, build servers, teams, projects, credentials, and administrative entry points; map compromise reach across them.
Protect dashboard access with HTTPS, strong authentication and available MFA, deliberate registration policy, and an appropriate restricted-access boundary.
Review actual team roles, invitations, removed members, service identities, and resource visibility; confirm intended boundaries with scoped accounts where authorized.
Keep API access deliberate and tokens appropriately scoped, attributable, revocable, and protected; verify installed-version permissions and access restrictions.
Review Git/source integrations and deployment hooks for caller authentication, target authorization, credential scope, and revocation without leaving stale triggers.
Distinguish the dashboard domain from direct management ports; restricting one route must not leave another public administrative path.
Verify required dashboard, realtime, terminal, remote validation, hooks, and certificate behavior before closing direct ports; account for self-hosted/controller/remote topology.
Secure remote-server SSH identities and verify effective sudo/Docker powers, trusted host identity, allowed sources, rotation, and recovery if the controller is lost.
Keep control-plane state, updates, encryption material, and recovery ownership explicit; losing access to its stored credentials can affect every connected server.
Separate untrusted builds/previews from sensitive workloads and management credentials; assess isolation at host, process, filesystem, identity, and network layers.
Inventory actual running container images/digests, users, capabilities, security options, mounts, networks, published ports, device access, and restart policies rather than only source Compose files.
Identify privileged containers, broad capabilities, host PID/IPC/network namespaces, host devices, and writable host mounts; justify or reduce each privilege through required behavior.
Restrict Docker socket/API access and equivalent control endpoints; read-only mounting or an application label alone may not create an effective privilege boundary.
Use an appropriate non-root workload identity and bounded writable locations where supported; verify file ownership, low-port needs, temp files, and health checks still work.
Review seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux and no-new-privileges/readonly constraints where compatible; document exceptions and validate the actual runtime rather than prescribing incompatible flags.
Check network membership and cross-project reachability; project separation in a dashboard does not establish denied container-to-container traffic.
Inspect external/shared networks, host aliases, direct database routes, and manually published ports that bypass domain routing or intended access controls.
Verify container DNS, outbound access, metadata/host access, and service discovery against intended workload authority and SSRF risk.
Bound CPU, memory, process counts, file descriptors, connections, storage, and log growth as required; inspect actual effective limits and their failure behavior.
Validate health/readiness, graceful shutdown, stop timeout, restart/backoff behavior, and service dependencies after deployment, crash, and host reboot.
Trace secrets through source integrations, build args, build context, environment files, image layers, logs, runtime environment, and frontend bundles; keep them out of public artifacts.
Separate production, staging, previews, and build identities/data; preview URLs and environment copies must not grant access to production providers or tenant data.
Review registry/source trust, image pinning, build tooling, install scripts, dependency updates, and native architecture; coordinate build provenance checks with module 05.
Verify the artifact and environment actually deployed, including configured branch/tag, build cache, runtime variables, and rollback image availability.
Inspect deployments that overlap old/new replicas for migration compatibility, concurrent startup jobs, duplicate consumers/schedules, and local-state assumptions.
Check proxy/route generation and manual overrides for drift, unexpected labels, wildcard collisions, stale routes, and configuration overwritten by the next deployment.
Verify failure/cancel paths leave an understood serving version and resource state; a successful build is not proof that startup, routing, or migrations succeeded.
Map every stateful path to a named volume, bind mount, external store, or intentional ephemeral path; identify data currently living only in a container layer.
Check volume ownership, UID/GID, mount location, permissions, disk/inode capacity, backup coverage, and behavior after container recreation or host replacement.
Verify cleanup jobs exclude required images, volumes, backups, deployment evidence, and rollback assets; never assume an unused label proves an artifact has no recovery purpose.
Monitor build/cache/image/log/volume growth and failed backup residue; prune only classified candidates with dependency and recovery evidence.
Detect orphaned preview environments, containers, routes, schedules, credentials, and billable resources; retire dependencies and external references together.
Establish a supported Coolify/Docker/proxy update process with backup, compatibility checks, maintenance impact, rollback limits, and post-update functional verification.
Demonstrate recovery of the management layer separately from application data; restoring a dashboard does not establish restored databases, uploads, or job ownership.
Confirm registrar/account ownership, contacts, strong authentication, recovery, transfer/registry locks where available, renewal payment, expiry, and external alert recipients.
Verify parent delegation, authoritative nameservers, zone availability, and agreement among authoritative servers; a correct record in an inactive dashboard is not effective DNS.
Review delegated subzones, in-bailiwick nameserver glue where relevant, abandoned secondary providers, and account ownership for each dependency.
Maintain a sanitized zone inventory/export and change history independent of a single dashboard; identify the authoritative configuration when UI/API/IaC can all modify records.
Scope DNS API credentials to required zones/actions and renewal/automation consumers; prevent unrelated workloads from changing production authority.
Review who can change nameservers, DS records, mail routing, ownership proofs, and certificate-validation records; those paths can bypass ordinary application controls.
Check availability dependencies and actual provider/service capabilities; several nameservers under one failing control plane are not automatically independent redundancy.
Review wildcard zones, internal split-horizon records, and search-domain behavior for accidental catch-all routing or private-name disclosure.
Reconcile A and AAAA with intended origins/edges and active firewall policy; remove stale/reassigned addresses only after checking legitimate consumers and recovery needs.
Inspect CNAME chains, dangling cloud/SaaS targets, abandoned verification records, and unclaimed resources for takeover or misrouting risk.
Verify apex/alias/flattening behavior and restrictions in the actual DNS service; do not assume one provider's pseudo-record semantics transfer unchanged.
Distinguish DNS-only and proxied records per hostname, supported protocol, certificate, and client; ordinary web proxying does not cover every port or non-web workload.
Evaluate origin disclosure through historical records, DNS-only subdomains, mail, certificate names, and alternate services; hiding the current A record is not an access control.
Verify wildcard, www/apex, administrative, preview, API, upload, and webhook hostnames each route to the intended protected service and TLS identity.
Check TTL and negative caching against failover/cutover expectations; changing a TTL does not retroactively expire answers already cached.

Validate from authoritative and selected recursive vantage points, including IPv4/IPv6 where relevant; explain caching, split-horizon, and geolocation differences rather than assuming immediate global agreement.
Verify SRV/TXT and other service-discovery records, ownership tokens, ACME delegation, and third-party verification still have a current owner and purpose.
Review CAA where selected for certificate-issuance policy, including subdomains, delegated challenges, wildcard issuance, and CA account/provider changes.
Where DNSSEC is selected and supported, verify signing, valid signatures, DNSKEY/DS chain consistency, algorithm support, and behavior with validating resolvers.
Monitor signature/key lifecycle and DS/signing drift; document accountable ownership for renewal, rollover, and incident correction.
Plan DNS-provider/nameserver changes with current DS/signing state and cache windows; stale parent trust can make an otherwise populated new zone fail validation.
Sequence key rotation, enabling/disabling signing, and registrar DS changes using provider-supported procedures; preserve a recovery path and validate externally after each relevant phase.
Keep DNSSEC's role distinct from encryption, registrar-account security, WAF filtering, and DDoS capacity; do not claim it prevents an authenticated malicious zone change.
Before transfer/cutover, export all required records and zone options, verify new authority, maintain required old service paths, and define rollback limits for cached/delegated state.
Verify the host/container resolver path, upstream availability, search domains, local cache, DNSSEC expectations, and timeouts under intended network policy.
If hosting an authoritative server, review zone transfer permissions, update authentication, recursion policy, TCP/UDP availability, response size, and upstream flood mitigation.
If running a recursive resolver, restrict authorized clients and review cache poisoning, forwarding, resource limits, and amplification exposure; ordinary applications need no public resolver.
Check large responses, truncation/TCP fallback, fragmentation/MTU effects, and resolver-specific failures with bounded queries where applicable.
Verify MX targets, priorities, address resolution, provider ownership, and retained mail routing; mail should not unintentionally expose a protected web origin or land on retired infrastructure.
Review SPF policy and include chains for actual senders and evaluation limits using current mail-provider guidance; remove obsolete authorizations without breaking legitimate delivery.
Verify DKIM selectors/keys, provider rotation, and alignment with the intended sending domains; distinguish configured DNS from actual signed message evidence.
Assess DMARC alignment, policy, reports, subdomain handling, and staged enforcement against legitimate senders; inspect real delivery before tightening policy.
For self-hosted mail, verify PTR/reverse DNS, forward identity, hostname/HELO, TLS, relay controls, blocked provider ports, reputation, and deliverability with module 14.
For non-sending domains, consider explicit non-sending mail policies according to actual domain/subdomain use and provider guidance; do not blindly apply a sending-domain template.
Keep account recovery and incident contacts reachable during a DNS/mail/hosting outage; test alternate access without exposing recovery secrets.
After changes, verify mail, OAuth ownership, ACME renewal, verification tokens, and service discovery as well as ordinary website resolution.
Inventory certificate names, issuers, termination points, private-key custody, expiry, automation, ownership, and dependent services; include dashboard, APIs, and non-web TLS.
Validate hostname/SAN, chain, trust, expiry, SNI, and certificate actually served at each required hop; a valid edge certificate does not prove origin validation.
Verify supported protocol/cipher policy against actual client requirements and current primary guidance; avoid hardcoded universal settings that break needed clients or age unnoticed.
Document the ACME challenge method, DNS/API credentials, renewal path, egress, ingress, and propagation prerequisites; certificate issuance and renewal must both work.
For HTTP-01, preserve the required port-80 validation path through all active proxies/firewalls and all answering origins; redirects and access gates must not break the challenge.
For DNS-01, verify TXT/delegation behavior, API scope, propagation, concurrent challenges, and cleanup; protect the automation credential as authority over relevant DNS.
Check wildcard versus explicit names, apex coverage, CAA policy, chosen CA limits, and staging/test issuance behavior against the actual ACME client/provider.
Monitor renewal execution and externally served expiry, including failed reloads, wrong storage permissions, full disk, lost account keys, and replicas serving different certificates.
Test supported certificate reload and key replacement paths where authorized; avoid assuming files on disk match the in-memory listener.
Prepare recovery for expired/revoked certificates, compromised keys, lost DNS credentials, and unavailable CA/provider without normalizing disabled verification.
Declare which hostnames permit direct origin traffic and which require trusted edge/tunnel ingress; record necessary health, ACME, administrative, and machine-client exceptions.
Validate encryption and identity checking on edge-to-origin connections; do not silently downgrade origin verification to solve a misconfiguration.
Enforce the chosen origin restriction at an effective layer, covering IPv4/IPv6, alternate ports, historic IPs, DNS-only names, and newly attached addresses.
Verify direct-IP/Host/SNI combinations and alternate names cannot reach protected apps outside intended ingress; a hidden origin address is not sufficient evidence.
If allowing an edge provider's IP ranges, update them through an owned validated process and recognize whether the rule identifies the provider network or the specific intended tenant.

Where specific origin authentication is required, verify the selected per-origin certificate/token/tunnel identity and its rotation/revocation; distinguish shared-provider identity from your own ingress authority.
For tunnels, inventory connector credentials, replica routing, local service binds, private routes, egress, access policy, and behavior when the connector or its control plane fails.
Reject unintended/default host routes and route collisions; distinguish legitimate SNI/Host rewrites from spoofed routing into another application.
Trust forwarded client-IP/protocol/host headers only from verified proxy hops; strip or normalize caller-supplied variants before using them for limits, logs, redirects, or secure cookies.
Inspect proxy-chain order, duplicate/conflicting forwarded values, PROXY protocol where used, and application trusted-proxy configuration; verify actual client attribution through every hop.
Validate redirects, external URL generation, cookie secure/domain attributes, OAuth callbacks, CORS, CSRF, and webhook destinations behind the real proxy topology.
Check HSTS host/subdomain/preload consequences only after all required names support the intended HTTPS behavior; define recovery implications before irreversible client caching commitments.
Review cache keys and cache-control for authenticated/personalized responses, tenant/locale variation, errors, redirects, cookies, and invalidation after access changes.
Verify WebSocket upgrades, SSE/AI streaming, response buffering, idle/total timeouts, compression, and disconnect behavior through the complete serving chain.
Check upload/body/header limits, request buffering, temporary disk, download/range requests, and large or slow clients against legitimate product requirements.
Inspect path normalization, encoded separators, duplicate headers, request framing, and HTTP-version translation where ambiguity could bypass routing/authentication or create request-smuggling risk.
Keep access/identity gates compatible with signed webhooks, bots, APIs, ACME, monitoring, and health probes; machine clients need deliberate protected paths rather than blanket browser challenges.
Verify edge/proxy error pages and maintenance modes do not disclose secrets, hide origin failure, cache privileged content, or report a healthy application when only an edge response works.
Version/record proxy configuration, middleware, labels, certificates, and external rules; identify which manual changes will be overwritten by Coolify or a later deployment.
Validate routing/config reload before and after proxy upgrades; define recovery for invalid configuration, conflicting routes, or lost certificate state.
Run bounded allowed/denied checks from appropriate paths and identify which edge/origin/version served the response; do not infer full-chain health from cached content.
Recheck TLS, origin restrictions, forwarded headers, renewal, and critical machine/user flows after DNS, CDN mode, IP, firewall, or ingress changes.
Separate registrar/DNS takeover, DNS amplification, network/transport floods, HTTP floods, credential abuse, scraping, expensive valid actions, and workload compromise in the threat model.
Verify the hosting account's actual upstream DDoS service, covered IPs/protocols, exclusions, detection/mitigation behavior, null-routing policy, contacts, and support escalation.
Record uncertainty in provider capacity and response guarantees; marketing descriptions and an enabled dashboard control are not evidence of surviving a specific attack.
Identify where a link, provider interface, host, proxy, database, worker pool, or paid provider saturates first; a local firewall cannot recover bandwidth already exhausted upstream.
Map protection by hostname, address family, port, and protocol; an HTTP edge/WAF may leave direct IP, UDP, mail, SSH, or other services outside its coverage.
Verify resilient authoritative DNS and no unintended public recursion/amplification service; web WAF configuration does not establish DNS-layer protection.
Determine whether origin restrictions prevent bypassing edge controls, including alternate names/ports/IPs and permitted exceptions.
Record actual WAF/bot/rate features and plan limits; do not assume a rule template or vendor feature name is available or enabled in this account.
Apply limits at appropriate identity levels: source network, account, tenant, session, token, route, expensive feature, and global budget; consider shared IPs and IPv6 address rotation.
Derive rate identities from verified proxy context; spoofed forwarding headers must not create unlimited fresh identities or ban innocent clients.
Bound authentication, password recovery, invitation, search, export, upload, image/media processing, AI, and other expensive paths according to cost and legitimate usage.
Verify quotas/concurrency remain effective across replicas, workers, retries, queues, and direct endpoints; process-local counters alone may not enforce a global budget.
Bound request bodies, headers, decompression, connection duration, idle clients, and simultaneous requests without breaking explicitly supported streaming or large-transfer routes.
Review cache-miss amplification, unique query strings, broad search/filter combinations, origin fetches, and unauthenticated cache bypass for disproportionate backend work.
Authenticate and validate webhooks/machine clients with deliberate protected exceptions; do not replace their verification with a blanket WAF bypass or browser-only challenge.
Check deny/challenge/rate responses, retry hints, account recovery, and accessible alternatives; false positives must be diagnosable and reversible.
Confirm limits preserve legitimate crawlers, login/OAuth, payments, uploads, ACME, monitoring, and assistive/client workflows using bounded representative checks.
Keep application authorization, input validation, and per-tenant controls behind the edge; passing a WAF does not confer authority or prove safe business behavior.
Define finite resource pools, queue bounds, admission control, backpressure, and shedding priorities; avoid unlimited buffering when a dependency slows down.
Measure relevant baseline latency/error distributions, bandwidth, connections, CPU, memory, disk/I/O, backlog, and provider spend; record dataset and workload context.
Account for builds, backups, log export, database maintenance, image pulls, and recovery competing with production; scheduled internal work can trigger the same saturation as external load.
Configure alerts and budgets for egress, paid API calls, autoscaling, storage/log growth, and retry storms; coordinate consequential spend controls with module 08.
Define an owned emergency sequence for tightening rules, disabling expensive features, queueing/read-only mode, or suspending abusive accounts with legitimate-user checks and rollback.
Keep provider escalation, off-host contacts, current instance/IP details, and a sanitized incident evidence procedure usable when the server is unreachable.
Compare edge/origin/application telemetry to locate the failing layer; distinguish blocked malicious traffic from origin outage and successful-but-expensive valid requests.
If capacity testing is explicitly authorized, define owned targets, source, maximum concurrency/rate/duration/cost, success criteria, stop conditions, and provider constraints before execution.
After mitigation, verify legitimate journeys, data/financial effects, backlog recovery, lasting rules, and credential/compromise concerns; do not close merely because traffic dropped.
Document residual risk, review triggers, and control ownership after real incidents, new expensive features, protocol changes, or material growth.
Define RPO/RTO and retention per critical data/service class, including what constitutes restored usable service; record accountable owners and accepted loss/downtime.

Inventory Coolify state, instance encryption material, application databases, uploads, named volumes, bind mounts, object stores, proxy/certificate state, DNS, infrastructure config, and required artifacts.
Distinguish control-plane backup from workload data backup; verify actual included files/databases, exclusions, job locations, and consumer expectations for each mechanism.
For self-hosted Coolify, preserve the matching APP_KEY securely outside the host separately from the instance database backup; verify custody without displaying its value.
Verify each application's engine/version supports the selected backup procedure; use appropriate native tools where the orchestration UI does not cover the required data.
Check backup consistency across live database transactions, files/blobs, multiple stores, and related application versions; a raw copy or VM snapshot is not automatically application-consistent.
Keep usable copies outside the source server/failure domain and review account/provider/region independence against the required disaster scenario.
Restrict backup credentials and deletion authority; consider versioning/immutability or independent custody when protection against malicious deletion is required and supported.
Protect encryption keys, password managers, recovery accounts, and decrypt permissions with an available off-host recovery path; encrypted backups without keys are not a recovery plan.
